entry.title: Continual Learning, Multi-task Learning
entry.content:
Introduction

Background and Motivation

Robots encounter new objects and tasks after deployment. Learning to open a drawer might help a robot learn to open a cabinet, but updating the model for the new task can also reduce its performance on earlier ones. This loss of previously learned behavior is called catastrophic forgetting.

Multi-task Learning

Multi-task learning (MTL) trains on several task datasets jointly so that related tasks can share representations and behaviors. Robotic datasets may differ in their sensors, embodiments, and simulation or real-world conditions. PoCo asks whether policies trained separately on these sources can share information at inference time without joint retraining.

Continual Learning and Catastrophic Forgetting

Continual learning (CL), or lifelong learning, trains on tasks in sequence with limited access to earlier data. It must balance plasticity, the ability to learn new skills, with stability, the ability to retain old ones. Keeping all past data for joint retraining would increase storage and training costs as tasks accumulate.

Characteristics Multi-task Learning Continual Learning
Task availability Simultaneous Sequential
Training data access Multiple task datasets Current task and potentially limited historical data
Training process Joint training Incremental learning
Primary objective Knowledge sharing across tasks Adaptation and retention
Major challenges Task interference and data heterogeneity Catastrophic forgetting and limited resources

Adaptation, Retention, and Knowledge Transfer

This lecture examines what a robot can reuse when learning a new task: training examples and parameters, policy predictions, or specialist skills.

Paper Knowledge Reuse Mechanism Primary Research Objective
LIBERO Benchmark methods that reuse demonstrations or protect parameters Measure transfer and forgetting across tasks
PoCo Compose independently trained policy predictions Use heterogeneous data without joint retraining
SRSA Retrieve and adapt specialist policies Learn new assembly tasks from existing skills

LIBERO: Benchmarking Knowledge Transfer for Lifelong Robot Learning

LIBERO is a simulation benchmark for lifelong robot learning. It provides 130 manipulation tasks, human demonstrations, and baseline algorithms and policy architectures for studying transfer and forgetting.

Figures are from the paper and supplement; captions are our summaries.

LIBERO: Motivation and Problem

After learning new tasks, a robot may fail to retrieve juice because it forgets the object’s location or the opening and grasping motions. LIBERO separates these sources of forgetting into declarative and procedural knowledge.

Type of knowledge What the robot needs to know Manipulation example
Declarative knowledge Object concepts, locations, and spatial relationships. Identify the juice and locate it inside the refrigerator.
Procedural knowledge Motions and behaviors needed to accomplish a goal. Open the door, grasp the juice, and retrieve it.

To isolate what transfers, LIBERO varies objects, spatial relationships, and task goals. It examines five questions:

  1. Knowledge transfer: Which task changes are hardest to learn and retain?
  2. Architecture: How should a policy combine images, language, robot state, and observation history?
  3. Learning algorithm: How do replay, regularization, and freezing affect learning?
  4. Task order: Do results change when tasks arrive in a different order?
  5. Pretraining: Does earlier training on a larger task set help?

LIBERO: Method and Formulation

Sequential learning setup

The robot learns \(K\) tasks in sequence. Each task \(\mathcal T_k=(\mu_0^k,g_k)\) specifies a starting-state distribution \(\mu_0^k\) and a success predicate \(g_k\). Tasks share state and action spaces and environment dynamics.

For task \(k\), the learner receives demonstrations \(D_k\). Earlier datasets are not fully available, though replay can retain selected examples. After each training stage, evaluation revisits earlier tasks to measure retention.

Generating tasks with explicit goals

The pipeline uses the Robosuite simulator:

  1. Generate instructions from Ego4D activity templates and available simulated objects.
  2. Specify the scene layout, object placements, and initial states.
  3. Define goal predicates in a PDDL-style task file. A drawer task, for example, succeeds when the drawer is open and the bowl is inside.

The predicates define success; the learned policy produces actions. Ego4D supplies language templates, while robot demonstrations are collected separately.

Four task suites

The paper uses four fixed suites for reproducible comparisons.

Task suite Tasks Main variation What it tests
LIBERO-Spatial 10 Locations and relations among the same objects. Distinguish identical bowls by their spatial relation.
LIBERO-Object 10 Target objects in pick-and-place tasks. Recognize and manipulate different object types.
LIBERO-Goal 10 Goals with fixed objects and layouts. Learn different motions and behaviors in one scene.
LIBERO-100 100 Objects, layouts, goals, and interactions. Transfer mixed knowledge across diverse tasks.

LIBERO-100 splits into 90 shorter tasks for pretraining (LIBERO-90) and 10 longer tasks for lifelong-learning evaluation (LIBERO-Long). Long horizon refers to dependent actions within an episode; lifelong learning refers to sequential training across tasks.

Policy architectures: from observations to actions

All three policies use external-camera and wrist-camera images, joint and gripper state, and BERT instruction embeddings. They differ in their visual encoder and temporal backbone; each has a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) action head.

Policy Visual encoder Temporal backbone Language integration
ResNet-RNN ResNet LSTM FiLM-conditioned visual features and a language input to the LSTM.
ResNet-T ResNet Transformer decoder FiLM-conditioned visual features and a language token in the temporal transformer.
ViT-T Vision Transformer Transformer decoder Language tokens in both visual and temporal transformers.

The temporal backbone summarizes the episode’s observation history. The GMM head predicts a distribution over continuous actions, from which the robot samples an action to execute.

ResNet uses language-conditioned FiLM to rescale and shift visual features, followed by spatial softmax and a linear projection. ViT uses self-attention over image-patch and language tokens. Both representations feed the temporal backbone.

Learning algorithms: preserving earlier skills

LIBERO pairs these architectures with three continual-learning algorithms and two reference methods.

Method How training works Resource or constraint
Sequential fine-tuning (SEQL) Train on the current task’s demonstrations only. No explicit retention mechanism.
Experience Replay (ER) Mix stored old-task examples with current data. Requires replay memory.
Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) Penalize changes using Fisher-based parameter importance. Constrains later updates.
PackNet Train, prune, fine-tune, and freeze task subnetworks. Leaves less capacity for later tasks.
Multi-task learning (MTL) Train jointly on all task datasets. Requires access to all datasets.

PackNet’s masks protect earlier subnetworks while allowing later tasks to use their frozen weights. MTL has full data access, so it serves as a joint-training reference rather than a guaranteed upper bound.

Demonstrations and training procedure

Policies are trained by behavioral cloning on 50 human demonstrations per task, collected through teleoperation with a 3Dconnexion SpaceMouse. A per-step negative log-likelihood loss is:

\[\mathcal L_{\mathrm{BC}}(\theta;D_k) =-\mathbb E_{(o_{\leq t},a_t)\sim D_k} \left[\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid o_{\leq t};\mathcal T_k)\right].\]

Source: Adapted from LIBERO, Section 2.2, Equation (2). This equation is not shown in the W13 presentation.

Here, \(\theta\) denotes policy parameters, \(o_{\leq t}\) is observation history, and \(a_t\) is the demonstrated action. Minimizing the loss increases the probability assigned to demonstrated actions.

The sequential evaluation procedure is:

  1. Train on the current task for 50 epochs using the selected algorithm.
  2. Evaluate every five epochs with 20 rollouts, each capped at 600 steps.
  3. Keep the earliest checkpoint with the best current-task success rate, then retest earlier tasks with 20 rollouts each.
  4. Continue through the task sequence and repeat with three random seeds.

PackNet adds 50 epochs of fine-tuning after pruning; the supplement reports metrics before this stage. MTL trains jointly. Separate studies vary task order and test LIBERO-90 pretraining before learning LIBERO-Long.

Evaluation equations from the W13 presentation

The slides use three success-rate metrics: forward transfer (FWT) for new-task learning, negative backward transfer (NBT) for forgetting, and area under the curve (AUC) for their combination.

The equations use the following notation:

Symbol Meaning
\(K\) Number of tasks in the sequence.
\(k\) Task being measured.
\(\tau\) A training stage after task \(k\).
\(e\in\mathcal E=\{0,5,10,\ldots,50\}\) The 11 evaluation checkpoints.
\(c_{i,j,e}\) Success rate on task \(j\) after \(e\) training epochs on task \(i\).
\(c_{i,j}\) Success rate on task \(j\) at task \(i\)’s selected best checkpoint.

Thus, \(c_{k,k}\) is task \(k\)’s best acquisition success rate, and \(c_{\tau,k}\) is its later performance. For these metrics, the learning curve is held constant after the earliest best checkpoint.

Forward transfer: learning a new task
\[\begin{aligned} \mathrm{FWT} &=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathrm{FWT}_k,\\ \mathrm{FWT}_k &=\frac{1}{11}\sum_{e\in\mathcal E}c_{k,k,e}. \end{aligned}\]

Source: W13 presentation, “LIBERO - Evaluation Metrics,” slide 29 (PDF page 38); LIBERO, Section 5.1, Equation (3).

FWT averages success across the 11 learning checkpoints, then across tasks. Higher values indicate faster or stronger learning. This definition does not subtract a from-scratch baseline, so it does not isolate the benefit of prior learning.

Negative backward transfer: forgetting an earlier task
\[\begin{aligned} \mathrm{NBT} &=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathrm{NBT}_k,\\ \mathrm{NBT}_k &=\frac{1}{K-k}\sum_{\tau=k+1}^{K} \left(c_{k,k}-c_{\tau,k}\right). \end{aligned}\]

Source: W13 presentation, “LIBERO - Evaluation Metrics,” slide 29 (PDF page 38); LIBERO, Section 5.1, Equation (3).

NBT averages the drop from task \(k\)’s best learned performance to its performance after later tasks. Lower values indicate better retention; negative values indicate improvement. A drop from 0.8 to 0.5 contributes 0.3.

Notation note: The inner expression applies to \(k<K\). For the final task, \(K-k=0\); computing the printed average requires a final-task convention.

AUC: combining learning and retention
\[\begin{aligned} \mathrm{AUC} &=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathrm{AUC}_k,\\ \mathrm{AUC}_k &=\frac{1}{K-k+1} \left(\mathrm{FWT}_k+\sum_{\tau=k+1}^{K}c_{\tau,k}\right). \end{aligned}\]

Source: W13 presentation, “LIBERO - Evaluation Metrics,” slide 29 (PDF page 38); LIBERO, Section 5.1, Equation (3).

AUC averages a task’s acquisition score, \(\mathrm{FWT}_k\), with its success rates after later tasks, then averages across tasks. The denominator counts one acquisition stage and \(K-k\) later stages. Higher AUC is better.

LIBERO: Experiments and Results

The authors evaluate how effectively different continual-learning algorithms acquire new tasks while retaining previously learned knowledge. The following table compares their performance on LIBERO-Long and LIBERO-Spatial using the evaluation metrics introduced above.

Method Long FWT ↑ Long NBT ↓ Long AUC ↑ Spatial FWT ↑ Spatial NBT ↓ Spatial AUC ↑
SEQL 0.54 0.63 0.15 0.72 0.81 0.20
ER 0.48 0.32 0.32 0.65 0.27 0.56
EWC 0.13 0.22 0.02 0.23 0.33 0.06
PackNet 0.22 0.08 0.25 0.55 0.07 0.63
MTL — — 0.48 — — 0.83

Sequential fine-tuning achieves the highest FWT on both task suites but also experiences the most catastrophic forgetting. On LIBERO-Long, it achieves an FWT of 0.54 but an NBT of 0.63, resulting in an AUC of only 0.15. This demonstrates that successfully learning new tasks does not necessarily imply that previously acquired knowledge is being retained.

Interestingly, Experience Replay achieves a higher AUC than PackNet on LIBERO-Long, whereas PackNet performs better on LIBERO-Spatial. This suggests that the effectiveness of a continual-learning algorithm depends on the type of knowledge being transferred. MTL outperforms the sequential methods in both comparisons, although it has access to all task datasets simultaneously.

The authors also investigate the relationship between policy architecture and continual-learning algorithm. The following table summarizes their AUC results on LIBERO-Long.

Policy architecture ER PackNet
ResNet-RNN 0.08 0.03
ResNet-T 0.32 0.25
ViT-T 0.25 0.34

ResNet-T outperforms ViT-T when using Experience Replay, but this ranking reverses when using PackNet. Therefore, policy architectures and continual-learning algorithms should be considered jointly rather than as independent design choices.

Finally, the authors investigate whether pretraining improves knowledge transfer. Policies are jointly pretrained on the 90 short-horizon tasks in LIBERO-90 using behavioral cloning for 50 epochs before sequentially learning the 10 tasks in LIBERO-Long.

Algorithm and architecture With pretraining Without pretraining
ER + ResNet-RNN 0.04 0.08
ER + ResNet-T 0.22 0.32
ER + ViT-T 0.10 0.25
EWC + ResNet-T 0.01 0.02
PackNet + ResNet-T 0.17 0.25

Contrary to expectations, pretraining reduces downstream performance across all five evaluated configurations. This suggests that knowledge acquired through standard supervised pretraining is not necessarily easy to reuse during continual learning. However, this finding is specific to the evaluated pretraining procedure and does not imply that pretraining is generally ineffective.

LIBERO: Limitations and Takeaways

Although LIBERO provides a structured benchmark for evaluating lifelong robot learning, there are several limitations to its experimental setup:

  • All experiments are conducted in simulation, which does not fully capture physical challenges such as sensor noise, disturbances, and uncertainty during manipulation.
  • Policies are trained using human demonstrations, limiting conclusions about robots that acquire knowledge through autonomous interaction and exploration.
  • The evaluation uses predefined task suites, which may not represent the diversity and unpredictability of open-ended lifelong learning.
  • Best-checkpoint selection relies on task-specific evaluation rollouts, which may not be practical for a continuously deployed robot.

The main takeaway from LIBERO is that learning more tasks does not necessarily translate to better lifelong learning. Sequential fine-tuning demonstrates strong adaptation but poor retention, while methods that prioritize retention may struggle to acquire new skills. Furthermore, the effectiveness of a continual-learning algorithm depends on both the policy architecture and the type of knowledge being transferred.

LIBERO’s primary contribution is therefore not a solution to catastrophic forgetting, but a standardized framework for understanding and measuring these tradeoffs. Its findings motivate further research into methods that explicitly encourage reusable knowledge while preserving previously acquired capabilities.

PoCo: Policy Composition from and for Heterogeneous Robot Learning

PoCo: Motivation and Problem

Why heterogeneous robot learning is difficult

Robots can learn manipulation skills from several useful sources: simulated demonstrations, human videos, and real robot teleoperation. Each source offers different strengths. Simulation provides large amounts of relatively inexpensive data, human videos are easy to collect and teach high level motions, and real robot demonstrations capture the actual robot’s contact rich interactions. However, these sources also differ in their data distributions, embodiments, control frequencies, and available sensors. Observations may include RGB images, point clouds, tactile images, or robot proprioception.

This creates a data heterogeneity problem: simply pooling all demonstrations into one training dataset is difficult, especially when the observation modalities and domains do not match. Training a separate specialist for every task or data source is possible, but those specialists do not automatically share their useful information. Meanwhile, collecting enough real robot data to cover every task and situation can be expensive.

PoCo (Policy Composition) asks: Can we train policies separately on heterogeneous data and combine their knowledge at inference time, without retraining a single model on all the data?

The paper focuses on generalizable robotic tool use, including hammering, scooping with a spatula, cutting, and using a wrench. The goal is to produce robust manipulation trajectories by combining information from different tasks, behaviors, sensing modalities, and data domains.

Core idea

Rather than forcing all data into one model, PoCo learns modular probabilistic policies using diffusion models. At test time, it composes these policies by combining their predictions over the same action trajectory space. This allows, for example, a policy trained with point clouds to be combined with one trained using RGB or tactile observations, or simulation knowledge to be combined with real robot demonstrations.

The important compatibility requirement is that the policies being composed must output trajectories with the same action dimension and horizon. Their observation inputs do not need to be identical. PoCo therefore offers a way to reuse independently learned skills and add new information without discarding previously trained policies.

PoCo: Method and Formulation

1. Represent each policy as a trajectory distribution

PoCo represents a robot policy as a probability distribution over action trajectories:

\[\pi(\tau \mid o)\]

Here, \(\tau\) is an action trajectory with horizon \(H\) and action dimension \(d\), and \(o\) is the robot’s observation (such as an image, point cloud, or tactile input).

Each policy is learned as a conditional diffusion model. During training, noise is added to expert action trajectories, and a neural network learns to predict that noise. At inference, the model starts with a noisy trajectory and repeatedly denoises it to generate an action sequence. The paper uses a mean squared error noise prediction objective:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MSE}} = \left\|\epsilon_t-\epsilon_\theta(\tau_0+\epsilon_t,t\mid o)\right\|^2\]

In this expression, \(\tau_0\) is the demonstrated trajectory, \(\epsilon_t\) is the noise added at diffusion step \(t\), and \(\epsilon_\theta\) is the learned noise prediction network. The key point is that the diffusion model represents a distribution of plausible robot trajectories, rather than outputting only one fixed action.

PoCo trains separate policies for different combinations of:

  • Modality \(M\): RGB image, point cloud, tactile image, or proprioception.
  • Domain \(D\): simulation, human demonstrations, or real robot data.
  • Task \(T\): the requested manipulation, such as hammering or scooping.
  • Behavior cost \(c\): an additional objective, such as smoothness or workspace safety.

2. Compose policies using a product of distributions

The central mathematical idea is probabilistic composition. Given two trajectory distributions, PoCo defines their composition as

\[p_{\mathrm{product}}(\tau)\propto p_1(\tau)\,p_2(\tau).\]

This product assigns high probability to trajectories supported by both policies. In other words, the composed policy favors trajectories that satisfy the information or requirements represented by each component.

The paper applies this idea in three main ways:

  • Task level composition: combines a general policy with task conditioned information, encouraging trajectories that accomplish a specified task. The paper uses a guidance weight to control how strongly the task condition influences generation.
  • Behavior level composition: combines a task policy with a cost function, so generated trajectories both perform the task and satisfy desired properties.
  • Domain level composition: combines policies trained on different domains or modalities, allowing their learned trajectory information to complement one another.

For behavior composition, a cost \(c(\tau)\) is converted into a probability like preference using a Boltzmann factor:

\[p_{\mathrm{cost}}(\tau)\propto \exp[-c(\tau)], \qquad p_{\mathrm{product}}(\tau)\propto p_{\mathrm{cost}}(\tau)\,p(\tau\mid T).\]

A lower cost therefore gives a trajectory higher probability. The paper gives smoothness and workspace bound constraints as examples.

3. Combine predictions during diffusion sampling

A product of distributions can be implemented by adding their corresponding score or energy gradient predictions. Intuitively, each component policy contributes a direction that guides the noisy trajectory toward regions it considers likely. The combined direction guides sampling toward trajectories supported by the composed policies.

For example, domain composition adds the predictions from two independently trained diffusion policies:

\[\tau^{t-1} = \tau^t-\gamma_D \left(\epsilon_{\theta_1}(\tau^t\mid t) +\epsilon_{\theta_2}(\tau^t\mid t)\right)+\xi.\]

Here, \(\tau^t\) is the current noisy trajectory, \(\gamma_D\) is a composition step size/weight, and \(\xi\) is Gaussian sampling noise. The same general procedure can include task guidance and gradients from behavior costs. The process repeats over denoising steps until a final trajectory is produced.

In short, PoCo does not merge the component networks’ parameters or retrain them jointly. It combines their trajectory predictions at inference time. This is what makes the approach modular: new policies or objectives can be added to the composition, provided their outputs use a compatible action trajectory representation.

PoCo: Experiments and Results

PoCo is evaluated on four tool-use tasks: scooping with a spatula, cutting with a knife, hammering, and turning a wrench. Simulation experiments use the Fleet-Tools benchmark with point-cloud observations, averaging 10 runs over 50 held-out scenes per task. Real-world experiments use a Franka Panda with wrist and overhead cameras and a GelSight tactile finger. The metric is task success rate.

Behavior and task composition

Adding smoothness or workspace costs at test time lowered each cost (smoothness from 0.027 to 0.016, workspace violation from 0.030 to 0.022) while success fell slightly, from 0.70 to 0.67, without retraining. Task composition, implemented as classifier-free guidance between conditioned and unconditioned multitask policies, outperformed both multitask baselines on all four tasks in simulation. On the real robot the results were more mixed:

Policy Spatula Knife Hammer Wrench Average
Single-task 8/10 8/10 5/10 5/10 65% ± 17%
Multitask, unconditioned 6/10 5/10 5/10 4/10 50% ± 8%
Multitask, conditioned 8/10 5/10 6/10 2/10 53% ± 25%
Multitask composition (\(\alpha = 2\)) 8/10 4/10 7/10 5/10 60% ± 18%

Composition was the best multitask approach, but separate single-task policies still had the highest average, and with 10 trials per task the differences fall within the reported standard deviations.

Domain composition

Domain composition produced the largest gains. On a real-world hammer-reaching task tested under four scene changes (5 trials each), composed policies outperformed each of their components:

Scene change Human Simulation Real robot Human + Real Sim + Real
Vary object pose 1/5 5/5 2/5 4/5 5/5
Vary robot and tool pose 1/5 5/5 4/5 5/5 5/5
Distractor objects 0/5 5/5 2/5 3/5 5/5
Novel object instance 1/5 3/5 2/5 1/5 5/5
Total 15% 90% 50% 65% 100%

In an ablation, pooling simulation point clouds and real images into a single model reduced success by 75% relative to composition, despite the larger model. Removing tactile input reduced success by 38%. Composition weights mattered throughout: performance peaked at intermediate values of \(\alpha\) and \(\gamma_D\).

PoCo: Limitations and Takeaways

PoCo combines policies at a single moment rather than sequencing them, so it was evaluated only on short-horizon tool use. All composed policies must share an action space and be roughly aligned in horizon, scale, and control frequency. Each denoising step evaluates every component, so inference slows as policies are added; two policies already limit control to 5 Hz. Composition weights are tuned by hand within a narrow stable range, policies still fail in delicate contact-rich tasks, and the evaluation is small: four tasks with 5 to 10 real-world trials per condition.

The main lesson is that heterogeneous data can be used by training separate policies and combining their predictions, which worked better than pooling the data into one network. For continual learning, this suggests a modular form of retention: existing policies are never updated, so new data or tasks cannot overwrite earlier skills, although the paper does not test this in a sequential benchmark. The costs are growing inference time and the need for compatible action spaces. SRSA also keeps a library of specialist policies but, instead of combining their predictions, retrieves the most relevant one and adapts its parameters to the new task.

SRSA: Skill Retrieval and Adaptation for Robotic Assembly Tasks

Motivation and Problem

While LIBERO investigates how robots acquire new knowledge while retaining previously learned capabilities, and PoCo explores how independently trained policies can be composed at inference time, SRSA introduces an alternative approach based on skill retrieval and adaptation.

Robotic assembly tasks, such as peg insertion, stacking, and mechanical component assembly, often require precise manipulation and contact-rich interactions. Training a new policy from scratch for every assembly task can be computationally expensive and sample-inefficient. However, previously learned assembly skills may contain transferable knowledge that can facilitate learning new tasks.

SRSA (Skill Retrieval and Adaptation) addresses this problem by maintaining a library of pretrained specialist policies. When encountering a new assembly task, the system retrieves a relevant existing policy and adapts it to the new task instead of learning entirely from scratch.

The central research question is:

How can a robot identify and reuse previously learned skills to efficiently solve unfamiliar assembly tasks?

Method and Formulation

The SRSA framework consists of three main components:

  • Skill Library: Stores pretrained specialist policies for previously learned assembly tasks.
  • Skill Retriever: Identifies existing policies that are likely to transfer successfully to a new task.
  • Skill Adapter: Fine-tunes a selected policy using reinforcement learning in a simulation environment.

Pretrained Skill Library

SRSA assumes that a collection of pretrained specialist policies is available before learning a new task. Each specialist is trained to perform a particular assembly task.

Conceptually, the skill library can be represented as

\[\mathcal{L} = \{(\mathcal{T}_i,\pi_i)\}_{i=1}^{N},\]

where $\mathcal{T}_i$ represents a previously learned assembly task, $\pi_i$ represents its corresponding specialist policy, and $N$ is the number of available policies.

Given a new target task $\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{new}}$, the objective is to identify an existing policy that provides a useful starting point for learning the target task.

Unlike conventional continual learning methods that repeatedly update a shared model, SRSA maintains separate specialist policies. This allows previously learned behaviors to remain available without directly modifying the original policies during adaptation.

Skill Retrieval

The skill retriever determines which pretrained policy is most suitable for a new assembly task.

Rather than selecting a policy solely based on the visual similarity between objects, the retriever estimates how successfully an existing policy can perform the target task.

Let $f_{\phi}$ denote a learned transfer success predictor parameterized by $\phi$. The predicted transfer performance of a source policy can be conceptually expressed as

\[\hat{s}_i = f_{\phi}(\mathcal{T}_i,\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{new}}),\]

where $\hat{s}_i$ represents the estimated transfer success of the specialist policy associated with task $\mathcal{T}_i$.

The retrieval objective can be simplified as

\[i^* = \arg\max_{i \in \{1,\ldots,N\}} \hat{s}_i.\]

The system identifies promising candidate policies and evaluates them in simulation before selecting a policy for adaptation.

An important challenge is that geometric similarity does not necessarily imply behavioral compatibility. For example, inserting a peg into a hole and placing a ring around a shaft may involve similar insertion motions but require different alignment and contact strategies. Consequently, an effective retriever must identify policies that provide transferable manipulation behaviors rather than simply recognizing similar objects.

Policy Adaptation

After retrieving a suitable specialist policy, SRSA adapts it to the target assembly task using reinforcement learning.

Instead of initializing the target policy randomly, the retrieved policy provides the initial parameters:

\[\theta_{\mathrm{new}}^{(0)} = \theta_{i^*},\]

where $\theta_{i^*}$ represents the parameters of the selected specialist policy.

The retrieved policy is subsequently fine-tuned using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). The general reinforcement learning objective is to maximize the expected discounted cumulative reward:

\[J(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_{\theta}} \left[ \sum_{t=0}^{H-1} \gamma^t r_t \right],\]

where

  • $\pi_{\theta}$ represents the parameterized robot policy.
  • $\tau$ represents a trajectory generated by the policy.
  • $H$ represents the trajectory horizon.
  • $\gamma$ represents the discount factor.
  • $r_t$ represents the reward received at time step $t$.

Through fine-tuning, the retrieved policy gradually adapts its behavior to the requirements of the new assembly task.

This approach allows the robot to begin learning with previously acquired manipulation knowledge rather than discovering the entire assembly strategy from scratch.

Adaptation and Retention

An important characteristic of SRSA is that it separates adaptation from retention.

  • Adaptation is achieved by fine-tuning the retrieved specialist policy for the new task.
  • Retention is achieved by preserving the original specialist policies in the skill library.

In contrast to sequential fine-tuning, where learning a new task may overwrite previously acquired knowledge, SRSA preserves existing policies while adapting a selected policy to the target task.

This separation provides an alternative approach to addressing the stability–plasticity dilemma in continual robot learning.

Experiments and Results

The authors evaluate SRSA on robotic assembly tasks and compare its performance with alternative learning approaches, including AutoMate, which learns specialist policies without SRSA’s proposed skill retrieval mechanism.

The experiments investigate whether retrieving a previously learned policy provides a better initialization for learning an unfamiliar assembly task.

The reported results demonstrate that SRSA improves learning performance compared with training policies from scratch. Retrieving a relevant specialist allows the robot to reuse existing manipulation knowledge, reducing the need to rediscover previously learned behaviors.

The main experimental findings can be summarized as follows:

Evaluation Aspect Main Finding
Skill retrieval Identifies previously learned policies that are promising candidates for transfer to new assembly tasks.
Policy adaptation Fine-tuning a retrieved policy can improve learning efficiency compared with training from scratch.
Task performance SRSA achieves better assembly performance than the evaluated AutoMate baseline.
Knowledge retention Previously learned specialist policies remain available while the selected policy is adapted.

These results suggest that explicit skill retrieval can facilitate knowledge transfer in robotic assembly tasks.

However, the effectiveness of this approach depends on the availability of relevant pretrained policies and an appropriate simulation environment for adaptation.

Limitations and Takeaways

Although SRSA demonstrates the benefits of retrieving and adapting previously learned skills, several limitations were identified during the lecture and classroom discussion.

Dependence on the skill library. SRSA assumes that a collection of relevant pretrained specialist policies is available. If a new task differs significantly from previously learned tasks, the skill library may not contain a suitable policy for adaptation.

Skill retrieval accuracy. Identifying transferable skills is challenging because assembly tasks with similar geometric structures may require different manipulation strategies. An inaccurate retrieval decision may provide an unsuitable initialization for subsequent learning.

Dependence on simulation. SRSA assumes that a simulation environment is available in which candidate policies can be evaluated and adapted. This assumption may limit its applicability to unstructured real-world environments where accurate simulation models are difficult to obtain.

Scalability. Maintaining separate specialist policies avoids directly overwriting previously learned behaviors. However, as the number of tasks increases, maintaining and searching an expanding skill library may introduce additional storage and computational costs.

Retrieval objective. A policy with high zero-shot success may not necessarily be the best policy for subsequent adaptation. A policy with lower initial performance could potentially adapt faster or achieve better final performance. This raises the question of whether retrieval should optimize initial success, adaptation efficiency, or final task performance.

Overall, SRSA provides an alternative perspective on knowledge reuse by retrieving and adapting pretrained specialist policies. While PoCo reuses policy predictions through composition and LIBERO evaluates knowledge transfer through continual learning, SRSA reuses previously learned policy parameters through retrieval and fine-tuning.

The key takeaway is that separating knowledge retention from adaptation can help robots preserve existing skills while efficiently learning new tasks. However, the effectiveness of this approach depends on the quality of the skill library, retrieval accuracy, and the availability of suitable environments for policy adaptation.

Discussion

The following summarizes questions from the audience and the discussion with the presenters. The exchanges are paraphrased from the class notes, with supporting paper details identified separately.

Attention maps and explainability

Audience question: Does LIBERO include attention maps, and can they explain how the robot interacts with objects?

Discussion with the presenters: Attention maps were not included in the presentation, but they appear in the paper’s supplementary material. They can highlight important objects or image regions, yet do not fully explain the details of interactions or the sequence of actions.

Paper context: These are perturbation-based saliency maps. The paper also reports similar-looking maps for ER and EWC despite different performance, illustrating the limits of using attention to explain behavior.

Overlapping object and spatial changes

Audience question: What happens when object identity and spatial arrangement change together, instead of being varied separately?

Discussion with the presenters: LIBERO-100 partially addresses this situation through tasks involving mixed changes. However, the discussion did not establish that it systematically covers every combination of object and spatial changes.

Paper context: LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Object emphasize individual factors, while LIBERO-100 includes mixed changes in objects, layouts, and goals.

Identifying important parameters

Audience question: How can freezing methods determine which parameters are important, when apparently minor weights may still contribute through less obvious interactions?

Discussion with the presenters: The concern was that parameter importance is difficult to interpret completely. An importance estimate may miss contributions that are not obvious from individual weights. This remained a question about the reliability of those estimates.

Paper context: PackNet has a concrete selection rule based on weight magnitude, followed by fine-tuning and freezing. Its masks protect retained old-task computation from later updates; the concern here is whether the selection preserves useful behavior before freezing.

Adding new tasks and reusing old data

Audience question: When a new task or new data is added, does learning also involve training on earlier data again?

Discussion with the presenters: Reusing old data is already covered by an approach evaluated in LIBERO. The discussion clarified that this is an existing mechanism for retaining earlier skills while learning a new task.

Paper context: Experience Replay (ER) mixes stored samples from previous tasks with demonstrations for the current task. It does not require retraining on the entire accumulated dataset from scratch.

Expert modules as a future direction

Audience question: Could the model reuse or add expert modules to learn new tasks while protecting earlier skills?

Discussion with the presenters: No specific expert-module approach was established in the discussion. Expert modules were raised as a possible direction for future continual learning research.

Paper context: LIBERO does not report a separate expert-module or mixture-of-experts baseline. PackNet already partitions a fixed network across tasks, but the benefits of adding separate experts are not established by these experiments.

entry.title: Human-in-the-loop Systems
entry.content:
Introduction

This lecture report covers the Human-in-the-loop Systems session in Learning for Interactive Robots (CS 6501, Fall 2026) at the University of Virginia.

The main question: When should a robot stop and ask a person for help?

Most robot learning puts the human at the start of the pipeline. People collect demonstrations or design a reward function, the robot trains, and after that the robot is on its own. A human-in-the-loop system keeps a person involved while the robot is actually running. That person might take over the controls, correct a mistake, or answer a question. Any of these makes the robot more reliable, and any of them costs the person time and attention.

That trade-off is the main design problem. A robot that asks too rarely fails in situations it was never trained for. A robot that asks too often isn’t saving anyone any work, since the person might as well do the task themselves. Striking the balance depends on the robot having a decent sense of its own uncertainty, which is hard for the large learned models robots use today. Diffusion policies and LLM planners can both be confidently wrong.

Overview of Papers

Both papers in this report are robot-gated, meaning the robot decides on its own when to ask for help. They differ in what kind of help the robot asks for and in how it measures its own uncertainty.

Diff-DAgger works at the level of motor control. A diffusion policy uses its own training loss to notice when its actions have drifted away from the expert data, then hands control to an expert who shows it what to do. Those corrections go into the dataset, and the policy is retrained on the bigger dataset before the next round.

KnowNo works at the level of task planning. An LLM planner writes out its possible next steps as a multiple-choice question and uses conformal prediction to figure out which options it can’t rule out. If more than one is left, it asks the human to pick. The LLM is never retrained. What the user gets instead is a statistical guarantee on how often the task succeeds.

  Diff-DAgger KnowNo
Level Low-level control High-level planning
Uncertainty signal Diffusion loss on the robot’s own action LLM confidence in each multiple-choice option
When the robot asks Loss stays above a threshold for $K$ steps in a row More than one option survives conformal prediction
What the human does Takes over and demonstrates Picks the correct option
What the help is used for Training data for the next DAgger round Finishing the current task
Guarantee None, results are empirical Task success of at least $1 - \epsilon$

Table 1: The two papers side by side.

Between them, the two papers cover two different reasons a robot might need a person. Diff-DAgger asks for help when the robot’s actions stop looking like the expert’s, and KnowNo asks when the robot can’t tell what the person meant.

Diff-DAgger: Uncertainty Estimation with Diffusion Policy for Robotic Manipulation

Imagine using behavioral cloning to teach a robot how to perform basic household tasks. Your training data contains many examples (demonstrations) of picking up cups of water. At test time, the robot goes to pick up a cup, but its grip begins slightly off-center. Because this case was never addressed in the demonstrations, the robot continues to grip with the same pressure, pushing the cup out of the gripper and onto the floor. All your investors are laughing, and your shoes are soaked.

Dataset aggregation (DAgger) aims to prevent catastrophes like these. The idea is to make the supervised training process more robust by allowing it to fill in its own gaps. After initial training, the robot is allowed to move in a simulated or real environment that can progress out of the training distribution. When the environment drifts far enough away from what the robot has been trained for, control is given to an expert – typically a human demonstrator – who steps in and corrects the action sequence. Then, the robot is re-trained with the new gaps filled in, and the process repeats.

While this technique works quite well in situations where reinforcement learning is infeasible (at least initially), a significant challenge is choosing when intervention should occur. As discussed in the following section, multimodal action distributions can make this process especially difficult. note that modern robot policies often use diffusion models to produce actions, from which they extrapolate an improved method for choosing when to intervene, which they call Diff-DAgger.

Motivation and Background

The key issue that caused the embarrassing investor demo in the introduction is called “covariate shift,” when actions taken by the agent result in shifted input variable distributions . Here is a summary of different DAgger methods:

Method Description
DAgger The original DAgger method. New labels are collected at out-of-distribution (OOD) states, and the dataset is re-aggregated.
Human-gated DAgger A human watches the robot take actions in its environment, then chooses when to intervene.
Robot-gated DAgger The robot decides when an intervention should happen, typically by estimating uncertainty.
Ensemble DAgger A robot-gated method that computes uncertainty as disagreement between multiple policies.

Figure 1 illustrates a key problem with Ensemble DAgger. At the multi-modal region where the agent must traverse the circle, two very different actions are possible: the agent may turn left or right. However, because different policies can choose either option, this would register as uncertainty, and the expert would be asked to intervene regardless of whether or not the robot was OOD.

proposes a new method for deciding when interventions should happen that uses a metric inherent to a popular policy architecture: diffusion models. Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPMs) work by iteratively producing a sequence of actions from noise. Its loss looks like

\[\mathcal{L}_\pi(o,a,\epsilon,t)=\left\|f(\epsilon,a,t)-f_\theta\!\left(o,\sqrt{\alpha_t}\,a+\sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\,\epsilon,\,t\right)\right\|^2,\]

where $\mathcal{L}\pi(o,a,\epsilon,t)$ represents the loss for a policy $\pi$ given observations $o$, an action label $a$, some noise $\epsilon$, and noising step $t$. The right-hand side simply calculates the distance between the diffusion model $f\theta$’s prediction and the training target $f(\epsilon,a,t)$ (the noise, the clean action, or a “velocity,” depending on how the model is trained) for the noised action label. The intuition of Diff-DAgger is that this loss function presents a better way to proxy uncertainty than asking multiple policies for potentially conflicting answers. Instead, the authors propose that the agent attempt to reconstruct its own action, the loss of which can provide a less-conflicting uncertainty estimate.

Method

The authors of Diff-DAgger use diffusion loss to estimate uncertainty. In order to compute loss in unseen states, they use the following estimation:

\[\mathcal{L}(o, a, \pi) = \mathbb{E}_{\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I),\; t \sim \mu(1, T)} \, \mathcal{L}_\pi(o, a, \epsilon, t).\]

In fact, this simply reuses the loss equation from earlier. The key idea is that the input action $a$ is now the action already generated by the model. If $\mathcal{L}(o, a, \pi)$ gives a loss higher than the $\alpha$ percentile observed in training for $K$ consecutive time steps, the robot will trigger an intervention. Because the action being scored is the one the policy itself generated, it already sits near one of the learned modes, so at a multi-modal decision point the loss stays low instead of being inflated by the other valid mode. This has an additional benefit over ensemble-DAgger: instead of running multiple policies at once, only one action needs to be computed at each time step.

Results

What We Are Testing

Robot-gated DAgger lets the robot decide when to ask an expert for help. This only works if the robot can tell when it is in trouble.

Diff-DAgger does this with one trick. A diffusion policy is trained to predict noise. At rollout time, we reuse that same training loss to score the action the robot just generated. A high loss means “this looks unlike my training data.”

The loss comes from the standard diffusion policy objective:

\[\mathcal{L}_\pi(o, a, \epsilon, t) = \left\| f(\epsilon, a, t) - f_\theta\!\left(o,\ \sqrt{\alpha_t}\,a + \sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\,\epsilon,\ t\right) \right\|^2\]

Here $o$ is the observation, $a$ is the action sequence, $\epsilon$ is Gaussian noise, and $t$ is the denoising step. Because $\epsilon$ and $t$ are random, the paper averages the loss over a batch of $N_b$ samples:

\[\bar{\mathcal{L}}(o, a, \pi) = \mathbb{E}_{\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I),\; t \sim \mu(1, T)} \; \mathcal{L}_\pi(o, a, \epsilon, t)\]

The decision rule has two knobs:

  • $\alpha$ is a quantile. We compute $\bar{\mathcal{L}}$ on every training pair. The $\alpha$-quantile of those values is the threshold.
  • $K$ is the patience. The expert takes over only if the loss exceeds the threshold for $K$ timesteps in a row.
\[\text{query at step } s \iff \bar{\mathcal{L}}(o_\tau, a_\tau, \pi) > q_\alpha \quad \text{for all } \tau \in \{s-K+1, \dots, s\}\]

The experiments ask three questions:

  1. RQ1. Can diffusion loss predict task failure?
  2. RQ2. With the same number of expert interventions, does Diff-DAgger beat existing methods?
  3. RQ3. Does it cut the wall-clock time of each DAgger iteration?

Tasks and Experts

There are three simulated tasks (built on ManiSkill) and two real-world tasks.

  • Stacking. Pick up a red cube and place it on a green cube. A basic perception and manipulation test.
  • Pushing. Use a stick to push a red T-shaped block to a target pose. This is contact-rich and needs multimodal planning.
  • Plugging. Insert a charger into a receptacle. This needs fine alignment.
  • Loading (real). Pick up soft bread and place it on a toaster. This tests handling deformable objects.

The simulated experts were designed on purpose. Stacking and plugging use a rule-based RRT motion planner, which plans over a long horizon. Pushing uses two RL agents trained with PPO. One is rewarded for rotating the object clockwise. The other is rewarded for counter-clockwise. They alternate when giving demonstrations, so the data truly has two modes for the same state. The authors also test learning from the counter-clockwise agent alone.

The real-world experts are humans teleoperating a robot with a VR controller.

Type Task # Obj # Cams Contact rich High precision Time limit Expert Avg. expert duration Expert success
Sim Stacking 2 3 No No 250 Motion planner 60.3 1.00
Sim Pushing 1 1 Yes No 250 RL agent 65.7 0.93
Sim Plugging 2 3 No Yes 500 Motion planner 147 0.98
Real Stacking 2 3 No No 600 Human 174.2 1.00
Real Loading 2 3 Yes Yes 600 Human 210.5 1.00

Table 2 (paper Table I): Task and expert summary. Time limits are in timesteps, at 20 Hz in simulation and 30 Hz in the real world.

Observations, Models, and Baselines

Cameras. Pick-and-place tasks use three cameras (left, right, in-hand) to avoid occlusion. Pushing uses one top-down camera. The real robot is a Franka Research 3 with three RealSense D435 cameras.

Model. All methods use the same diffusion policy: a U-Net head with FiLM conditioning. The paper tests two input types:

  • State-based. Robot joint positions, end-effector pose, and the true object poses.
  • Image-based. An R3M ResNet18 encoder with spatial softmax, plus proprioception. Random crop augmentation is used.

The observation horizon is set to one to keep batches small. The diffusion model uses V-objective prediction (see “Choosing the Prediction Target” below).

Task Action space Initial demos Final demos New demos per update $\alpha$ $K$ $N_b$
Stacking (sim) Abs. pose 20 60 4 0.99 2 512
Pushing (1 expert) Rel. joint 20 100 4 0.99 1 512
Pushing (2 experts) Rel. joint 20 100 4 0.9 2 512
Plugging Abs. pose 20 100 8 0.99 2 512
Stacking (real) Abs. pose 40 120 20 0.99 2 512
Loading (real) Abs. pose 40 120 20 0.99 2 512

Table 3 (paper Table IV, trimmed to the DAgger columns): Key hyperparameters.

Baselines. Three comparisons, all using the same diffusion policy so expressiveness is equal:

  • Behavior Cloning (BC). Train once on offline demonstrations.
  • Ensemble-DAgger. Five policies. Their disagreement (action variance) measures uncertainty.
  • ThriftyDAgger. A strong robot-gated method. It adds a learned risk estimate on top of the ensemble.

RQ1: Can Diffusion Loss Predict Task Failure?

Why Ensembles Struggle: A Toy Example

Before the robot tasks, the paper uses a 2D navigation problem. An agent goes from start to goal around a circle. It can go clockwise or counter-clockwise. Both are correct, so the data has two modes.

Look at the left chart. The ensemble’s disagreement is highest at the fork, which is a normal, in-distribution spot. It is even a bit higher than in the truly out-of-distribution region. Each policy is confident, they just pick different paths. The ensemble reads that as uncertainty.

Now the right chart. Diffusion loss is low and nearly equal for the single-mode region and the fork. It jumps only in the out-of-distribution region. That is exactly the behavior we want.

The Evaluation Setup

For each task, the policy is trained on enough demos to land near a 50% success rate. Then it runs 100 random episodes with no expert help. For each episode, we record two things: did the task fail, and did the robot ask for help? All methods use the same $\alpha$ and $K$.

We then report standard scores:

\[\text{TPR} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}, \qquad \text{TNR} = \frac{TN}{TN + FP}, \qquad F_1 = \frac{2\,TP}{2\,TP + FP + FN}, \qquad \text{Acc} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN}\]

TPR is the share of failing episodes where the robot asked for help. TNR is the share of successful episodes where it stayed independent.

Results

    Ensemble-DA 0.81 0.31 0.52 0.59

    Ensemble-DA 1.00 0.11 0.60 0.73

Table 4 (paper Table II): Query decisions versus task outcomes over 100 rollouts, visuomotor tasks.

Diff-DAgger has the best F1 and accuracy on every task. The paper reports averages across the simulated visuomotor tasks:

  • Against Ensemble-DAgger: +42.7% F1 and +38.4% accuracy.
  • Against ThriftyDAgger: +22.6% F1 and +32.8% accuracy.
  • Across all tasks, the abstract summarizes this as a 39.0% gain in failure prediction.

Notice the pattern in the baselines. Ensemble-DAgger and ThriftyDAgger often have a TPR of 1.00 but a TNR near zero on single-expert pushing. They ask for help almost every time. On two-expert pushing, the picture flips for Ensemble-DAgger: a TPR of 0.29 means it misses most failures.

Videos. The authors’ project page shows diffusion-loss behavior on two tasks. (We link them rather than copy them.)

Video 1: Stacking with diffusion loss (source, project page).

Video 2: Pushing with diffusion loss (source, project page).

RQ2: Does the Collected Data Make a Better Policy?

Here every method gets the same number of expert demonstrations. We then train a final policy on the collected data and measure success rate. Simulation uses 100 evaluation episodes. Real-world tasks use 20.

  Stack (sim)   Push (1 exp.)   Push (2 exp.)   Plug   Stack (real) Load (real)
  State Image State Image State Image State Image Image Image
BC 0.89 0.85 0.89 0.72 0.74 0.71 0.75 0.49 0.60 0.80
Ensemble-DA 0.72 0.83 0.87 0.81 0.70 0.59 0.69 0.37 – –
Thrifty-DA 0.79 0.86 0.85 0.81 0.69 0.68 0.65 0.47 – –
Ours 0.94 0.94 0.96 0.87 0.87 0.79 0.92 0.84 0.80 0.95

Table 5 (paper Table III): Success rate after the final DAgger iteration. Ensemble and Thrifty were not run on the real robot.

Three things stand out:

  • Diff-DAgger wins every column. On average it gains 13.7% over the second-best method in state-based tasks. In visuomotor tasks, including real-world ones, the average gain is 25.2%. (The introduction reports 20.6% overall.)
  • The baselines can lose to plain behavior cloning. Stacking from state: BC gets 0.89, Ensemble-DAgger 0.72. Plugging from images: BC 0.49, Ensemble-DAgger 0.37. Interactive data was worse than offline data.
  • It works on real hardware. Real stacking goes from 0.60 (BC) to 0.80. Loading goes from 0.80 to 0.95.

The authors’ real-world demonstration video is on the project page:

Video 3: Real-world demonstration (source, project page).

RQ3: Is It Faster?

Yes. The Ensemble approach pays three costs that Diff-DAgger avoids:

  1. Training. Five policies must be trained. Diff-DAgger trains one.
  2. Threshold setting. Ensemble methods run full ensemble inference on the entire training set. Diff-DAgger passes a single batch per data point.
  3. Inference. Five forward passes versus one.
Speedup of Diff-DAgger over Training Threshold setting Inference
Ensemble-DAgger 5.1× 48× 3.8×
ThriftyDAgger 6.4× 53× 3.9×

Overall, the policy update time drops by a factor of 7.8 versus Ensemble-DAgger. A full update takes only about 0.54 hours. ThriftyDAgger is slower still, because it collects extra data and trains a separate risk estimator.

False Positives vs. False Negatives

The two kinds of query mistakes do not cost the same.

  • A false positive means the robot asks for help it did not need. You lose some of the benefit of interactive learning. In the worst case, you are just doing offline imitation.
  • A false negative is worse. The robot is overconfident and fails. It then drifts into states far from the useful data.

Ensemble-DAgger and ThriftyDAgger both make many false negatives, especially with two pushing experts. The authors’ guess: the training data already has high action variance, because the two experts disagree in the same state. That makes the ensemble numb to real out-of-distribution states. The authors also suspect this is why those baselines sometimes fall below behavior cloning. (This is a speculation in the paper, not a tested claim.)

Diff-DAgger has far fewer false negatives across tasks. That is the better trade for interactive learning with messy, multimodal data.

Seeing the Difference: The Plugging Task

  • Diff-DAgger (top). The charger starts to slip, and the robot asks for help at 9.1 s. The expert steps in and the episode succeeds.
  • ThriftyDAgger (middle). The robot keeps trying after the slip. It only asks at 14.7 s, after dropping the charger.
  • Ensemble-DAgger (bottom). The robot makes no progress and never asks. It times out at 25.0 s, and the system forces an expert in.

The authors’ plugging video is here:

Video 4: Plugging (source, project page).

Choosing the Prediction Target

Diffusion models can be trained to predict different targets: the noise $\epsilon$, the clean sample, or a “velocity” (V-objective). The paper notes that this choice affects both convergence speed and final performance. They found that sample and V-objective prediction converge faster than epsilon. They use V-objective everywhere, since it balances convergence and performance.

An Unexpected Bonus: Recovery Behavior

Policies trained on Diff-DAgger data sometimes recover from their own mistakes. The robot misaligns the cube, fails, tries again, and succeeds. This kind of behavior usually shows up only if someone carefully plans recoveries into offline data. Here it appears naturally. The authors link it to the policy-performance gain over offline training. The mechanism makes sense: the expert steps in right at the moments of trouble, so the dataset ends up full of “how to fix it” examples.

Limitations

Stated by the authors:

  1. Diffusion policies are still slow to train. Diff-DAgger removes the ensemble cost, but a diffusion policy takes longer to train than a simpler policy class. The authors hope faster computing will ease this.
  2. Speed was bought with trade-offs. Many choices that speed up training (such as a one-step observation horizon) cost some policy performance. The authors plan to look at this in future work.

Our reading of what remains open (not claims from the paper):

  1. Thresholds are set by hand. $\alpha$ and $K$ differ by task (for example, 0.9 for two-expert pushing and 0.99 elsewhere). Picking them well may need tuning.
  2. Strong baselines in the real world are missing. Ensemble-DAgger and ThriftyDAgger were only run in simulation (Table 5), so real-world comparisons are against BC alone.

Takeaways

Diff-DAgger is a robot-gated DAgger method that reuses a diffusion policy’s own training loss as an uncertainty signal. In the paper’s experiments:

  • It predicts task failure better than Ensemble-DAgger and ThriftyDAgger.
  • It handles multimodal demonstrations, where ensemble disagreement gets confused.
  • Its collected data trains better policies, in simulation and on a real Franka robot.
  • It cuts wall-clock time per policy update by 7.8× versus Ensemble-DAgger.

The core idea is simple. A model trained to denoise expert actions is naturally surprised by actions unlike the expert data. That surprise is a cheap and well-behaved query signal.

KnowNo: Robots That Ask For Help

Say you ask a kitchen robot to “put the bowl in the microwave.” There are two bowls on the counter, one plastic and one metal. The robot’s language model planner reads the instruction, picks the metal bowl with total confidence, and puts it in the microwave. Now there are sparks coming out of the microwave, and the robot is waiting for its next instruction.

As far as the planner could tell, the plan was fine. The problem is that the instruction was ambiguous, and nothing in the planner was built to notice that. Large language models (LLMs) are good at turning instructions into step-by-step plans, but they also hallucinate: they give answers that sound reasonable, are wrong, and come with high confidence. Instructions from people make this worse, since we leave out details all the time, sometimes on purpose and sometimes without realizing it.

propose KnowNo (“Know When You Don’t Know”), a way for an LLM planner to figure out when it should stop and ask a person for help. Like the robot-gated DAgger methods above, the robot is the one deciding when a human gets involved. What changes is the kind of help. In Diff-DAgger, the expert takes over the low-level controls. In KnowNo, the human answers a question about the plan (“Which bowl did you mean?”) and the robot keeps going on its own.

The authors call their goal uncertainty alignment, which has two parts:

  1. Calibrated confidence. The user picks a success rate $1 - \epsilon$, and the robot asks for enough help to reach it, with a statistical guarantee.
  2. Minimal help. Out of all the ways to reach that success rate, the robot should ask as few questions as possible.

A robot that asks about everything meets the first goal and misses the second. A robot that never asks misses the first. KnowNo uses conformal prediction to balance the two.

Related Work

Area What prior work does Where KnowNo differs
LLM planners SayCan and similar systems turn language instructions into multi-step robot plans. These planners have no way to ask for clarification. When the instruction is ambiguous, they guess.
Asking through prompting Inner Monologue feeds scene descriptions and human feedback back into the prompt, which lets the LLM ask questions. Getting the robot to ask the right amount takes a lot of prompt engineering, and there is no way to know ahead of time how often the robot will succeed.
Uncertainty estimates for LLMs Many papers try to calibrate an LLM’s confidence in a single answer. A calibrated score for one answer still doesn’t tell the robot which other answers to consider. Conformal methods return a set of answers with a coverage guarantee instead.
Conformal prediction for LLMs apply conformal prediction to multiple-choice question answering. That work assumes the answer options are given. KnowNo has the LLM write its own options, so it works for open-ended planning.
Conformal prediction in robotics Earlier robotics work uses conformal prediction for fault detection, trajectory prediction, and planning around moving obstacles. Those guarantees either hold on average at each step or are very conservative. KnowNo calibrates over entire plans, so the guarantee covers the whole task even though each action changes what the robot sees next.

How KnowNo Works

Step 1: Planning as Multiple Choice

The obvious way to measure an LLM’s confidence in a plan step $y$ is the probability it assigns to the whole sentence, $p(y)=\prod_{i=1}^{k}p(\sigma_i \mid \sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{i-1})$, where $\sigma_1, \dots, \sigma_k$ are the tokens in the step. The trouble is that this product shrinks as the sentence gets longer. “Put the plastic bowl in the microwave” scores lower than “put bowl in microwave” for reasons that have nothing to do with which one is correct.

KnowNo gets around this with a multiple-choice trick. KnowNo prompts the LLM to generate candidate next steps, formatted as multiple-choice question answering (MCQA) with options A–D and an added “E: an option not listed here” choice. The prompt includes a text description of the scene (from an object detector, or given directly), the user’s instruction, and a few example options from other scenarios. The LLM is then asked which option is correct. The LLM’s next-token probability for each letter serves as its confidence in that option. We write this score as $\hat{f}(x)_y$, the confidence in label $y \in \mathcal{Y} = {A, B, C, D, E}$ given the prompt $x$. Every option is now a single token, so length stops mattering.

Option Plan Score $\hat{f}(x)_y$
A Put the plastic bowl in the microwave 0.46
B Put the metal bowl in the microwave 0.41
C Put the plastic bowl in the sink 0.08
D Put the metal bowl in the sink 0.03
E An option not listed here 0.02

Table 6: MCQA scores for “put the bowl in the microwave” (made-up numbers for illustration, not from the paper).

The LLM leans toward A, but only slightly. Picking the top option here is close to a coin flip between the two bowls. The next step decides whether a lean like that is good enough to act on.

Step 2: Conformal Prediction

Using a calibration set of example scenarios, conformal prediction finds a confidence threshold that achieves a user-specified success level $1 - \epsilon$. In more detail:

  1. Collect $N$ example scenarios and label the correct option for each one. The paper uses $N = 400$.
  2. For each scenario, compute the nonconformity score $\kappa_i = 1 - \hat{f}(x_i)_{y_i}$. This is one minus the LLM’s confidence in the correct answer, so a high $\kappa_i$ means the right answer surprised the LLM.
  3. Set $\hat{q}$ to the $\frac{\lceil (N+1)(1-\epsilon) \rceil}{N}$ empirical quantile of $\kappa_1, \dots, \kappa_N$.

At test time, every option scoring above the threshold goes into a prediction set:

\[C(x_{\text{test}}) = \{\, y \in \mathcal{Y} : \hat{f}(x_{\text{test}})_y \geq 1 - \hat{q} \,\}\]

Conformal prediction guarantees that the correct option lands in this set with probability at least $1 - \epsilon$:

\[\mathbb{P}\big(y_{\text{test}} \in C(x_{\text{test}})\big) \geq 1 - \epsilon\]

The intuition is that $\hat{q}$ is picked so that in roughly $1 - \epsilon$ of the calibration scenarios, the correct answer scored at least $1 - \hat{q}$. A new scenario comes from the same distribution, so its correct answer should clear the same bar just as often. This holds whether or not the LLM’s scores are any good. A poorly calibrated LLM just ends up with bigger sets, which means more questions. If the scores do match the true probabilities, the sets are also the smallest possible for that success level, which is where the minimal help goal comes in.

One detail: the guarantee above is an average over random draws of the calibration set. The paper uses a stronger version that holds for the specific calibration set you collected (with probability $1 - \delta = 0.99$), so the robot doesn’t need a fresh calibration set for every new task.

Back to the example: if calibration gave a threshold of $1 - \hat{q} = 0.30$, the prediction set would be {A, B}. The sink options are ruled out, but the robot still can’t tell which bowl you meant.

Step 3: Asking for Help

  • If the set contains exactly one option, the robot executes it.
  • If the set contains more than one option, the robot asks the human to choose. The options are turned into a plain-language question, like “Should I put the plastic bowl or the metal bowl in the microwave?” If the right answer is E, the human describes the correct action instead.

Assuming the human always answers correctly, the robot can only fail when the correct option is missing from the set. That happens at most $\epsilon$ of the time, so the task success rate is at least $1 - \epsilon$. In other words, the coverage guarantee from conformal prediction turns into a task success guarantee.

Multi-Step Plans

Most tasks take more than one step, which breaks a key assumption of conformal prediction: that every data point is independent. In a multi-step plan, what the robot sees at step $t$ depends on what it did at earlier steps.

KnowNo handles this by calibrating on whole plans instead of single steps. A plan with steps $t = 0, \dots, T-1$ gets the score of its weakest step:

\[\hat{f}(\bar{x})_{\bar{y}} = \min_{t} \hat{f}(x^t)_{y^t}\]

where $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$ are the sequences of prompts and correct labels. Calibration runs on these sequence scores and produces a single threshold $\hat{q}$. At test time the robot can’t see future steps, so it builds a prediction set at each step using that same $\hat{q}$. The authors prove that these step-by-step sets contain exactly the same plans as a set built from the whole sequence at once. So if the robot asks for help whenever any step’s set has more than one option, the $1 - \epsilon$ guarantee covers the entire task rather than each step separately.

The paper also extends this to cases with more than one acceptable option, like “bring me a soda” when there is both a Coke and a Sprite on the table. In that setting, the guarantee is that the set contains at least one acceptable option.

Experimental Setup

Four environments spanning simulation, single-arm manipulation, mobile manipulation, and bimanual coordination:

Environment Task Ambiguity
Simulation: PyBullet Tabletop Rearrangement A simulated robot arm rearranges colored blocks and bowls on a tabletop Attribute, numeric, spatial
Hardware: Multi-Step Tabletop Rearrangement (UR5 arm) A physical UR5 arm with a suction gripper sorts 28 toy food items into blue and green plates based on human dietary preferences Only a subset of preferences is given
Hardware: Mobile Manipulator in an Office Kitchen A mobile robot operates in an office kitchen with a countertop, drawers, a microwave, and waste bins Spatial, safety
Hardware: Bimanual Tabletop Manipulation (dual Kuka IIWA 7 arms) Two arms with limited reachability must coordinate object handovers and bin sorting Vague commands (e.g., which arm should act)

Baselines

KnowNo was primarily evaluated with PaLM-2L as the base planner, and compared against:

Baseline Description
Simple Set Adds options in order of LLM confidence until their total reaches $1 - \epsilon$, without calibration
Ensemble Set Same as Simple Set, but scores come from how often the LLM picks each option across 20 randomized prompts
Prompt Set Asks the LLM to list the prediction set directly
Binary Asks the LLM to say whether it is certain or uncertain
No Help Always executes the top-scoring option

KnowNo Results

  1. Reliable task success guarantees. In simulation, with a target success level of 85% ($\epsilon = 0.15$), KnowNo had the smallest deviation from the target across all three ambiguity settings. The uncalibrated baselines either missed the target or gave the user no way to set one.
  2. Minimizing human help rate. For the same success level, KnowNo asked for help less often than the baselines. The gap grew as instructions became more vague. Ensemble Set also performed well, but needed more inference time.
  3. Quantitative hardware performance. On the UR5, KnowNo reduced human help by 14% per step and 8% per trial compared to Simple Set. On the mobile manipulator, it reduced help by 14%. Overall, KnowNo reduced human help by 10–24% compared to the baselines.
  4. Ablation on scoring functions. Replacing the MCQA letter scores with sentence-level scores (raw sentence probability or perplexity) made performance worse, especially when candidate options varied a lot in length. Scoring a single letter avoids this length bias.

Conclusions

Conformal prediction paired with MCQA allows operators to tune a statistical guarantee on task completion, while keeping human help to a minimum. KnowNo works with off-the-shelf LLMs without fine-tuning.

The key limitation is that the guarantee currently assumes:

  1. The environment’s scene state is accurately parsed into text.
  2. Low-level robotic controllers execute the selected primitive without failure.
  3. The human always answers correctly. The method does not account for human error, so a wrong answer from the human breaks the guarantee.

In addition, calibration requires a labeled dataset of scenarios. The authors used 400 examples, which took about 4 hours to label in the multi-step setting, and this must be repeated for each new environment.

Student Q&A

KnowNo

Q: How can robots learn from past clarifications to reduce repeated questions and adapt to individual users?

A: Maybe we can create a memory bank of human clarifications. The next time a similar situation is faced, we can retrieve the past record from the memory bank, to reduce the frequency of asking the same question in the future.

Q: What role could another LLM play in helping robots resolve uncertainty, and when would human clarification still be necessary?

A: Perhaps another LLM could be used to help resolve uncertainty. The 2 models can discuss with each other, and if an agreement can’t be reached, they can ask a human for help. This may make the decision process slower, and may ultimately end up just following the decision of the stronger LLM. If the LLMs are about equal, then the additional LLM does not really help.

Q: How can KnowNo be adapted when the calibration set differs in distribution from the deployment environment?

A: Several studies mention how we can dynamically change the calibration set for the application.

Diff-DAgger

Q: If diffusion loss measures how well an action matches the learned distribution rather than whether the action will succeed, is diffusion loss alone sufficient for reliable failure prediction?

A: No, because diffusion models just measure how an action matches the distribution of the dataset. It measures the uncertainty of the robot. However, if an action is not in the distribution, that does not necessarily mean it failed the task.

Q: What types of expert interventions would be most valuable for improving a robot’s policy?

A: Motion planner interventions may be more optimal than human expert interventions, but human expert interventions may be more diverse. There’s a tradeoff between the two. A motion planner can help you find the shortest trajectory, but a human expert can help reach out-of-distribution states (helping the policy to be more generalized). This paper has humans intervene when the policy is uncertain (the action hasn’t been executed yet), but it is also important to learn how to recover from failure. If demonstration data only includes successful trajectories, the robot doesn’t learn how to recover from failure. However, failing on purpose can also cause cost and safety problems. It is an interesting problem to consider whether to intervene before or after failure.

Model Uncertainty

Q: What does it mean for a robot to be uncertain? How is uncertainty different from the risk of task failure?

A: Uncertainty can mean a lot of things, such as unsafe or unwanted actions. The definition of uncertainty depends on the situation or environment the robot is in.

Sources

  • Lee, Kang, Kuo. Diff-DAgger: Uncertainty Estimation with Diffusion Policy for Robotic Manipulation. ICRA 2025. arXiv:2410.14868
  • Project page and videos: diffdagger.github.io
  • Ren et al. Robots That Ask For Help: Uncertainty Alignment for Large Language Model Planners. CoRL 2023. arXiv:2307.01928
  • Project page: robot-help.github.io
