entry.title: Shared Autonomy: Aligning Robot Assistance with Human Intent

link.title: Shared Autonomy: Aligning Robot Assistance with Human Intent

entry.content:
Introduction

A robot can execute movements that are difficult for a person to specify directly, yet the person usually understands what they want better than the machine does. Shared autonomy aims to combine these complementary strengths: a human supplies goals, preferences, and corrective inputs, while an autonomous controller helps translate those inputs into successful actions.

The challenge is not simply to maximize the amount of automation. A six-degree-of-freedom robot arm is awkward to operate with a low-dimensional joystick, especially when a task requires both reaching for an object and manipulating it precisely. A racing driver, meanwhile, may know whether they intend to overtake a car but lack the reaction time to steer optimally through a difficult corner. In either setting, a technically competent intervention can become counterproductive if it conflicts with the person’s actual objective.

This lecture examined two complementary approaches. Dream2Assist predicts a driver’s discrete tactical intent and learns corrective actions that advance that intent . Latent Actions + Shared Autonomy (LA+SA) instead learns a low-dimensional control interface whose meaning changes with the robot’s belief about the user’s goal . Together they motivate a central question: How can assistance become more capable while preserving the user’s ability to express, revise, and ultimately control their own objective?

Shared Autonomy and Its Challenges

Shared autonomy lies between pure teleoperation, in which the human commands the machine, and full autonomy, in which the machine selects and executes actions independently. One common implementation blends a human command $a_h$ with a robot-proposed command $a_r$:

\[a=(1-\alpha)a_h+\alpha a_r,\qquad 0\leq\alpha\leq1.\]

Here, $\alpha=0$ corresponds to direct human control and $\alpha=1$ to full robot control. This convex blend is the formulation used by LA+SA; Dream2Assist uses a related but distinct add-and-clip rule for steering and acceleration. In either case, determining an appropriate robot action requires more than deciding how much control to assign to the machine.

Two problems recur throughout the lecture. First, intent is partially observed: a robot sees joystick motions or vehicle controls, not the human’s underlying plan. Second, the control interface is constrained: the human’s input may have far fewer degrees of freedom than the robot, and small mistakes can be amplified during high-speed or fine-motor tasks. The methods below respond to different parts of this difficulty—one learns which correction to make, and the other learns what a human command should mean.

Dreaming to Assist

DeCastro et al., “Dreaming to Assist: Learning to Align with Human Objectives for Shared Control in High-Speed Racing” (CoRL 2024).

Motivation and problem formulation

In high-speed racing, the assistant must support tactical decisions before there is time for explicit communication. A driver might try to pass an opponent, stay behind, or pass from the left rather than the right. These choices can demand conflicting control actions: slowing down is helpful for staying behind but may frustrate an attempted overtake.

The paper formulates control as a two-player partially observable decision process. The assistant observes features of the track, the ego and opponent vehicles, and the human’s steering and acceleration. The human’s objective $y$ is latent. Both controllers output normalized continuous actions $a_t^H,a_t^A\in[-1,1]^2$; the vehicle receives their coordinate-wise sum, clipped to its admissible control range:

\[a_t^{\mathrm{exec}}=\mathrm{clip}(a_t^H+a_t^A,-1,1).\]

Thus, success means more than making the vehicle fast or safe in isolation. The intervention should improve task performance while remaining consistent with the driver’s intended maneuver.

Method: an intent-aware world model

Dream2Assist builds on Dreamer, a model-based reinforcement learning approach that learns a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) and trains policies using imagined trajectories . The RSSM combines a deterministic recurrent state $h_t$ (memory of recent interactions) with a stochastic latent state $z_t$ (uncertainty about the environment). Observation, reward, and continuation heads predict what the world might do next. Dream2Assist adds an intent-prediction head $p_\phi(y_t\mid h_t,z_t)$, training the representation to encode not only vehicle dynamics but also the objective underlying the observed human actions.

The training pipeline has three stages:

Stage 1. (Construct diverse synthetic drivers) Train separate policies for passing, staying behind, left-biased driving, and right-biased driving. Save intermediate checkpoints to represent varying levels of skill, rather than only expert behavior.

Stage 2. (Learn an assistant across this population) Train its RSSM to predict dynamics, rewards, and discrete intent; train an actor–critic policy on model-generated rollouts. This is a form of fictitious co-play: the assistant learns to work with many plausible human partners.

Stage 3. (Deploy the assistant online) Infer the driver’s current objective from their behavior and apply continuous steering and throttle corrections appropriate to that objective.

The assistant’s reward incorporates three competing considerations: common driving objectives (finishing, avoiding collisions, staying on track), a penalty on large interventions, and alignment with the inferred human objective. The intervention term is

\[r_t^{\mathrm{interv}}=-\|a_t^A\|_2.\]

Importantly, the model can evaluate a proposed action using the predicted reward of an expert driver with the inferred intent. The paper also explores an expert-action matching term, but the results discussed in the lecture use expert-reward alignment, since direct expert-action matching performed worse. This distinction helps explain why correctly classifying intent need not be enough: the assistant must also model the consequences of its actions.

Experiments and results

Evaluation was conducted in the CARLA simulator on two sections of Thunderhill Raceway: a relatively easy 370 m straightaway and a harder 960 m hairpin section. The experiments separately contrasted pass vs. stay-behind and left vs. right preferences, averaging outcomes over five imperfect synthetic drivers. Baselines included ordinary Dreamer, which lacks intent-aware reward alignment, and Dreamer-AIL, an adversarial imitation-learning assistant without the same RSSM-based intent-aware planning structure.

The evaluation tracked change relative to unassisted driving in track progress, human-objective return, and collisions. The most informative findings were:

  • (In difficult hairpin settings, Dream2Assist improved track progress by roughly 27–72 m in the reported conditions), without increasing collisions, while also better satisfying the simulated driver’s preferred maneuver.
  • (Skill level mattered.) Imperfect drivers generally benefited most. More capable drivers often needed smaller corrections, and extra intervention could occasionally reduce their performance.
  • (Generic assistance could optimize the wrong behavior.] Dreamer sometimes favored staying behind an opponent even when the driver wished to pass, while Dreamer-AIL could freeze, collapse toward a single maneuver, or drive too aggressively.
  • (Intent accuracy did not guarantee useful help.) Intent classification achieved approximately 0.95–1.00 F1 in the lecture’s reported tests. A non-RSSM ablation could classify intent nearly as well, yet assisted less effectively—suggesting the importance of learned dynamics and reward predictions.

A more demanding test swapped synthetic drivers mid-race to simulate a sudden change in intent. Classification performance initially fell, then recovered to high accuracy after approximately 4–8 seconds. This shows some adaptability, but also exposes a potentially significant lag in a high-speed setting.

Limitations

The evaluated 2024 system was trained and tested with synthetic human policies, not real drivers sharing control in the reported experiments. Its set of tactical intents was small and predefined, and the opponent vehicles replayed recorded trajectories rather than adapting to the driver. The approach also depended on expert models for each known objective. These choices make the method controlled and interpretable, but leave open questions about natural human behavior, novel objectives, multi-agent interactions, and the safety of assistance during intent transitions.

Shared Autonomy with Learned Latent Actions

Jeon, Losey, and Sadigh, “Shared Autonomy with Learned Latent Actions” (RSS 2020).

Motivation: reaching is not manipulating

Assistive feeding illustrates a different limitation of conventional shared control. A user must first move a robotic arm toward an item, then perform a precise manipulation—cutting tofu, stabbing a marshmallow, or scooping through icing. Simple goal-directed assistance is useful during the first phase but insufficient during the second. At the same time, asking someone to manipulate every degree of freedom of a robot arm with a two-dimensional joystick is cumbersome.

The key insight is that the meaning of a low-dimensional input should depend on context. Early in a task, pushing a joystick can communicate which object to approach. Once the robot is confident about the object, that same joystick movement can instead express how to manipulate it. The transition is learned through a context-conditioned latent-action decoder, rather than through explicit manual switching between control modes.

Method: belief-conditioned decoding and shared guidance

Let $s$ denote the robot configuration, $z\in\mathbb{R}^d$ the joystick input, and $a\in\mathbb{R}^m$ the robot action, with $d<m$. Let $\mathcal{G}$ contain candidate discrete goals, and let $b(g)$ be the robot’s belief that $g$ is the intended goal. The learned decoder converts low-dimensional input into a high-dimensional action:

\[a_h=\phi(z,s,b).\]

The robot independently proposes goal-weighted guidance, then blends that guidance with the human’s decoded command:

\[a_r=\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}b(g)(g-s),\qquad a=(1-\alpha)\phi(z,s,b)+\alpha a_r.\]

The decoder $\phi$ is trained offline on demonstrated trajectories containing states, actions, and goal beliefs. Online, each joystick input is decoded using the current state and belief; the controller then computes assistance, executes the blended action, and updates its belief based on the user’s behavior.

Interactive intuition: confidence and assistance

The visualization below illustrates how the belief over goals and the assistance weight play different roles. Increasing $b(g_1)$ redirects the goal-weighted autonomous suggestion toward goal 1; increasing $\alpha$ gives that suggestion more influence in the executed command. The human-action arrow is held fixed in this simplified demonstration—it is not a reproduction of the paper’s learned decoder, whose behavior also changes with belief.

Why train for goal accessibility?

There is an important failure mode: once a robot becomes confident in the wrong target, both its autonomous guidance and a poorly trained latent space may reinforce that mistake. If the decoder provides no actions that move toward an alternative goal, the user cannot correct the robot merely by moving the joystick.

The paper studies this trade-off using the goal error $e(t)=g^{\ast}-s(t)$ and a Lyapunov function $V(t)=\tfrac12|e(t)|^2$. Under the paper’s stated bounded-control assumptions, a sufficient condition for decreasing error is

\[b(g^{\ast})\|e\|\gt\sigma_h+\big(1-b(g^{\ast})\big)\sigma_r,\]

where $\sigma_h$ bounds the human’s decoded command and $\sigma_r$ bounds the influence of competing goals. Greater confidence in the correct goal tightens the region toward which the robot converges; confidence in an incorrect goal can instead make switching difficult. This is a sufficient condition for local progress, not an unconditional global convergence guarantee.

To make alternative goals reachable, the authors add an entropy term during offline decoder training:

\[\mathcal{L}=\|a_{\mathrm{demo}}-\hat a\|_2^2 +\lambda\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}p_{(s,b)}(g)\log p_{(s,b)}(g).\]

Here, $p_{(s,b)}(g)$ measures the relative accessibility of each goal through the available latent actions; it is not the same quantity as the posterior goal belief $b(g)$. Since $\sum_g p(g)\log p(g)=-H(p)$, minimizing the loss rewards a decoder that reconstructs demonstrations and preserves multiple possible goal-directed motions. In simulations, this design helps a user undo an earlier mistake or switch to a newly preferred target.

Simulations and user study

The simulation studies examined imperfect teleoperators, changing goals, people learning a control interface during a task, and targets not seen during training. LA+SA generally reduced reaching error and completion time, especially for noisy users. LA+SA with entropy was more resilient when a simulated user changed goals after the robot had developed a confident but incorrect belief. New targets were handled by mapping the unfamiliar context to an equivalent familiar one and transforming the decoded action back, rather than retraining the decoder.

The physical-robot study recruited 10 able-bodied participants, each using a 2-DoF joystick to operate a 7-DoF robot arm in two eating tasks (tofu and a multi-step dessert). The experiment compared four conditions: direct retargeting (R), retargeting plus shared autonomy (R+SA), latent actions alone (LA), and the combined LA+SA method.

Results supported the complementarity of the two components:

  • Shared autonomy improved goal accuracy across tasks, with a reported main effect of $F(1,18)=29.9$ and $p<0.001$.
  • Latent actions enabled changes in fine-grained manipulation preferences. Participants could move between stabbing, scooping, and dipping motions rather than remaining in one default manipulation pattern.
  • The combination was most efficient: LA+SA produced the lowest total and idle times among the tested conditions, with reported pairwise comparisons at $p<0.05$.

These results provide human-participant evidence that shared guidance and a learned control interface solve distinct problems. Nevertheless, the study was small, recruited only able-bodied participants, and used a restricted family of feeding tasks and demonstrated motions; deployment to the broader population of assistive-robot users would require additional evaluation.

Comparison and Key Takeaways

Although these systems operate in very different domains, their successes and failures point to a common design principle: automation should help realize the human’s objective without removing the human’s ability to choose or change it.

Dimension Dream2Assist Latent Actions + Shared Autonomy
Domain High-speed driving Assistive robot manipulation
Main uncertainty Which discrete maneuver the driver intends Which goal the user wants, and which continuous manipulation they prefer
Learned mechanism Intent-aware RSSM plus assistive policy Context-conditioned low-dimensional action decoder
How assistance acts Steering/throttle corrections added to human control Goal-weighted guidance blended with decoded joystick commands
Characteristic failure Wrong maneuver inferred or excessive corrections Incorrect goal belief makes alternatives unreachable
Key response Intent-conditioned expert reward and intervention penalty Belief-conditioned decoding and entropy-based goal accessibility
Core evidence in lecture Synthetic-driver CARLA experiments Simulations and a 10-participant eating study

Three lessons emerge. First, the assistant should represent why a person acts, not merely imitate the resulting action: two visually similar driving situations may require opposite interventions. Second, confidence must be coupled with reversibility: even a very confident model must leave a practical path for the human to correct it. Third, greater assistance is not automatically better. The appropriate intervention depends on task difficulty, user skill, uncertainty, and the cost of suppressing alternatives.

Open Questions and Discussion

The lecture concluded with questions about when assistance becomes over-assistance. Several are especially important for designing future systems:

  1. If a driver signals an overtake that appears unsafe, should the assistant optimize for the intended maneuver, delay it, or override it? What should trigger that decision?
  2. Dream2Assist can take several seconds to recover after a simulated intent switch. How should an assistant behave while its estimate is unreliable, especially in a fast-changing environment?
  3. A latent action may coordinate many robot joints at once but be hard for a human to interpret. Could online adaptation, feedback, or more interpretable constraints make the interface easier to learn?
  4. Should we measure intervention magnitude, goal error, successful human corrections, subjective agency, or all of them? How would these metrics change across users and tasks?
  5. How would the systems scale to unfamiliar intents, reactive opponents, new objects, or users whose control patterns vary substantially from training data?

A natural direction is to combine the two ideas: use a predictive model to maintain uncertainty over human objectives and a latent control interface designed to preserve controllable escape routes when that uncertainty is wrong. Such a system would not treat confidence as permission to eliminate alternatives; it would learn to assist while remaining corrigible to the user’s next action.

Discussion 1: Human vs. Robot Control During Accidents

Our first discussion focused on when an autonomous vehicle should transfer control to a human driver, particularly in situations involving unavoidable or imminent accidents. Some participants argued that control should be returned to the human because people might be able to exercise judgment, improvise, or at least minimize the damage. Others suggested that the autonomous system should remain in control because robots can process sensor information and react faster than humans, especially in emergencies where delayed reactions can make the situation worse. An unexpected handover could also be dangerous if the human does not have enough time to understand the situation and respond appropriately.

We concluded that the appropriate allocation of control depends heavily on the specific scenario, rather than following a universal rule. Important considerations include the time remaining before a collision, the driver’s awareness, the reliability of the autonomous system, and whether either party can realistically improve the outcome. This connects to Dreaming to Assist, which emphasizes understanding human intent while maintaining safe and effective assistance. One possible approach is for the autonomous system to handle immediate safety-critical corrections while allowing meaningful human intervention whenever sufficient time and information are available. However, the paper’s experiments were conducted in simplified racing simulations, so its findings do not establish how control should be transferred during real-world traffic emergencies.

Discussion 2: Shared Autonomy in Assistive Robots for Older Adults

Our second discussion appears to have concerned how much autonomy assistive robots should have when helping older adults or people with limited physical abilities perform everyday tasks. The presentation used robotic feeding as an example, where a user controls a high-dimensional robotic arm through a relatively simple joystick. The paper Shared Autonomy with Learned Latent Actions demonstrated how robots can interpret limited human inputs and translate them into more complex movements, including reaching toward food and performing precise actions such as cutting, stabbing, or scooping. This raises a fundamental tradeoff between improving task efficiency through automation and preserving the user’s ability to control the robot according to their own preferences.

A primary concern is that excessive robotic assistance may reduce human agency, particularly when the robot incorrectly predicts what the person wants. For example, a feeding robot might assume that the user wants to pick up a particular food item and continue moving toward it even after the user attempts to change direction. Conversely, requiring complete manual control could be physically demanding and frustrating. The slides suggest that effective shared autonomy should adapt assistance to the person’s abilities, confidence, and changing intentions while keeping alternative actions accessible. The broader question is therefore not simply whether robots should perform more tasks autonomously, but how they can provide useful assistance without unnecessarily restricting human choice, independence, and dignity.

References

  • DeCastro et al. (2024), Dreaming to Assist: Learning to Align with Human Objectives for Shared Control in High-Speed Racing. CoRL 2024.
  • Jeon, Losey, and Sadigh (2020), Shared Autonomy with Learned Latent Actions. RSS 2020.
  • Hafner et al. (2019), Learning Latent Dynamics for Planning from Pixels. ICML 2019.
entry.summary: How should a robot help without fighting its user? We study intent-aware assistance in high-speed racing and belief-conditioned latent actions for assistive manipulation, comparing their methods, evidence, and limitations.

entry.title: Social Interaction, Cooperation
entry.content:
Introduction

Topic Overview: Multi-agent coordination, game-theoretic formulations of human-robot teaming, and social conventions in shared workspaces.

This lecture report covers the Social Interaction, Cooperation session in Learning for Interactive Robots (CS 6501, Fall 2026) at the University of Virginia.

Multiple robots work together to achieve higher goals. But building a multi robot/agent system does not simply mean putting multiple robots or agent together. It often requires 3 Cs: Coordination， Cooperation, Collaboration.

Structures of multi-human/robot interaction:

Roles of interaction:

  • supervisor
  • Operator
  • Teammate
  • Mechanic/Programmer
  • Bystander
  • Mentor
  • Information Consumer
  • The roles are quickly evolving: assistant shared autonomy, etc

Why do robots need social skills:

  • Robots are leaving the lab and entering shared spaces: Robots will work in an environment with humans
  • People are not obstacles: Robot needs to interact with human
  • Intent is hidden: Robot has to infer why human acts
  • Handover and shared workspace: Robot may replace or collaborate with human

This leads to today’s problem in two angles:

  • How should a robot reason about other agents’ goals?
  • Where does human-aware behavior come from

Social interactions as recursive MDPs

Motivation

Social interaction requires reasoning recursively about how another agent’s goals instead of only focusing on the goal itself. For example, both robots want to water the same tree themselves. Sharing this physical destination does not imply cooperation: one robot may also try to prevent the other from completing its task. A robot that only infers where its partner is going can therefore miss why that partner acts. Recognizing an intention to hinder changes how it should respond.

Motivated by the need to equip robots with social skills and the ability to infer other agents’ social goals, this paper introduces Social MDPs to give such interactions an explicit planning formulation. An agent combines a physical goal, concerning what it wants to accomplish in the environment, with a social goal, concerning another agent’s reward. Helping and hindering become objectives that can be balanced against the agent’s own task and action costs. Because the other agent may also reason socially, this formulation requires nested estimates of goals and rewards.

Background

Markov Decision Process (MDP). An MDP models sequential decisions when the agent observes the current state. It can be written as

\[\mathcal{M}=\langle S,A,T,R\rangle,\]

where \(S\) and \(A\) are state and action spaces, \(T(s'\mid s,a)\) gives transition probabilities, and \(R(s,a)\) specifies reward. A policy \(\pi(a\mid s)\) selects actions to maximize expected cumulative reward. In the standard MDP, the reward represents the physical goal of the agent.

Partially Observable MDP (POMDP). When the state is not directly observable, the model adds observations:

\[\mathrm{POMDP}_i =\langle S,A_i,T_i,\Omega_i,O_i,R_i\rangle.\]

Here, \(\Omega_i\) is the observation space, and \(O_i(o_i\mid s',a_i)\) gives the probability of an observation after action \(a_i\) leads to state \(s'\).

Interactive POMDP (I-POMDP). I-POMDPs is the extensions of POMDPs that recursively model other agents’ beliefs about the state of the world. An agent reasons about what another agent believes, including that agent’s beliefs about other agents. This supports predicting actions based on the other agent’s perspective and available information.

The two-agent formulation is:

\[\mathrm{I\text{-}POMDP}_i =\langle IS_i,A,T_i,\Omega_i,O_i,R_i\rangle, \qquad IS_i=S\times M_j.\]

Here, \(IS_i\) is the interactive state space, combining the physical state \(S\) with possible models \(M_j\) of agent \(j\). The action space \(A=A_i\times A_j\) contains joint actions. Agent \(i\) maintains a belief over interactive states; when its model of \(j\) includes \(j\)’s beliefs about agent \(i\), the belief structure becomes recursive.

Connection to Social MDPs. I-POMDPs recursively model agents’ beliefs about the world state, whereas Social MDPs recursively model their estimated reward functions. Social MDPs use this reward dependence to express helping and hindering while keeping physical states fully observable.

Method

1. Social MDP For agent \(i\) interacting with agents in \(J\), a Social MDP describes its physical task and social objectives, with a maximum reasoning level \(l\). The model is defined as:

\[M_i^l=\langle S,A,T,\chi_{iJ},g_i,R_i^l,\gamma\rangle.\]
  • \(S\) is the environment’s state space, with \(s\in S\) denoting a particular state.
  • \(A=A_J\) is the joint action space of the agents in \(J\). Each agent chooses an individual action \(a_i\in A_i\), and \(a_J\) collects the actions taken by all agents.
  • \(T(s'\mid s,a_J)\) gives the probability of reaching state \(s'\) from state \(s\) after the joint action \(a_J\).
  • \(\chi_{iJ}\) collects agent \(i\)’s social goals toward the other agents. Each \(\chi_{ij}\) describes its social objective with respect to agent \(j\ne i\), such as helping or hindering that agent.
  • \(g_i\) is agent \(i\)’s physical goal.
  • \(R_i^l\) is agent \(i\)’s reward function at reasoning level \(l\). It incorporates the agent’s estimates of other agents’ rewards.
  • \(\gamma\in(0,1)\) is the discount factor controlling the weight of future rewards.

2. Recursive reward. The immediate reward of an agent \(i\) at level \(l\) is computed as follows:

\[\begin{aligned} R_i^l(s,a_J,\chi_{iJ},g_i) &=r_i(s,a_i,g_i)+\sum_{\substack{j\in J\\j\ne i}} \chi_{ij}\!\left( \widetilde R_j^{i,l-1} \left(s,a_J,\widetilde\chi_{jJ}^{i,l},\widetilde g_j^{i,l}\right) \right)-c(a_i). \end{aligned}\]
  • \(r_i(s,a_i,g_i)\) is the physical reward associated with agent \(i\)’s own goal \(g_i\).
  • \(c(a_i)\) is the cost when agent \(i\) takes action \(a_i\).
  • \(\widetilde R_j^{i,l-1}\) is agent \(i\)’s estimate of agent \(j\)’s reward, treating \(j\) as a level \(l-1\) agent.
  • \(\widetilde\chi_{jJ}^{i,l}\) represents agent \(i\)’s estimates, at reasoning level \(l\), of agent \(j\)’s social goals toward other agents.
  • \(\widetilde g_j^{i,l}\) is agent \(i\)’s estimate, at reasoning level \(l\), of agent \(j\)’s physical goal.
  • \(\chi_{ij}\) transforms agent \(j\)’s estimated reward into a contribution to agent \(i\)’s reward. The framework permits an arbitrary transformation.

This paper uses a linear transformation, written here as \(\chi_{ij}(x)=w_{ij}x\):

  • \(w_{ij}>0\) favors helping, as increasing agent \(j\)’s estimated reward benefits agent \(i\).
  • \(w_{ij}<0\) favors hindering, as decreasing agent \(j\)’s estimated reward benefits agent \(i\).
  • \(w_{ij}=0\) removes the social reward contribution associated with agent \(j\).

The magnitude of \(w_{ij}\) controls the importance of the social objective relative to the physical reward. A stronger social weight can justify additional action costs, while a weaker weight may leave the agent prioritizing its own physical task.

3. Planning for Social MDPs. Planning combines the agent’s immediate reward with the expected consequences of future interactions. The state-action value is defined as:

\[\begin{aligned} Q_i^l(s,a_J,\chi_{iJ},g_i)=R(s,a_i,\chi_{iJ},g_i)+\gamma\sum_{s'\in S} T(s,a_J,s')V_i^l(s',\chi_{iJ},g_i). \end{aligned}\]

Here, \(R\) denotes the immediate reward defined above. The transition notation \(T(s,a_J,s')\) denotes the same probability as \(T(s'\mid s,a_J)\). To evaluate future states, agent \(i\) must account for uncertainty about the partner’s goals and actions. The expectation of Q-value is:

\[\begin{aligned} V_i^l(s',\chi_{iJ},g_i) &=\max_{a_i'\in A_i} \mathbb{E}_{\widetilde g_j^{i,l},\widetilde\chi_{jJ}^{i,l},a_j'} \left[Q_i^l(s',a_J',\chi_{iJ},g_i)\right]. \end{aligned}\]

The expectation uses the inferred probabilities of the partner’s physical and social goals, together with its estimated policy.

3.1 Updating social and physical goals of other agents. At time \(t=0\), the model uses uniform distributions over candidate physical and social goals. At subsequent steps, it updates these estimates using observed behavior and the partner’s estimated policy from the previous time step.

Social-goal update. The belief about the partner’s social goal is updated as:

\[\begin{aligned} &P\!\left(\widetilde\chi_{ji}^{i,l,t} \mid s^{t-1},a_J^{t-1}\right)\propto P\!\left(\widetilde\chi_{ji}^{i,t-1} \mid s^{t-2},a_J^{t-2}\right)\times \sum_{\widetilde g_j^{i,l,t-1}} P\!\left(a_j^{t-1}\mid s^{t-1}, \widetilde\chi_{ji}^{i,l,t-1},\widetilde g_j^{i,l,t-1}\right)\times T(s^{t-1},a_J^{t-1},s^t). \end{aligned}\]
  • \(\widetilde\chi_{ji}^{i,l,t}\) is agent \(i\)’s estimate, at level \(l\) and time \(t\), of agent \(j\)’s social goal toward \(i\).
  • The previous belief is reweighted by the likelihood of the observed action \(a_j^{t-1}\), summing over candidate physical goals \(\widetilde g_j^{i,l,t-1}\).
  • \(T(s^{t-1},a_J^{t-1},s^t)\) accounts for the transition produced by the previous joint action.

Physical-goal update. The physical goal is inferred from the observed state history while marginalizing over the unknown social goal:

\[\begin{aligned} &P\!\left(\widetilde g_j^{i,l,t}\mid s^{1:t-1}\right)\propto \int_{\widetilde\chi_{ji}^{i,l,t}} P\!\left(s^{1:t-1}\mid \widetilde g_j^{i,l,t},\widetilde\chi_{ji}^{i,l,t}\right)\cdot P\!\left(\widetilde g_j^{i,l,t}\right) P\!\left(\widetilde\chi_{ji}^{i,l,t}\right) \,d\widetilde\chi_{ji}^{i,l,t}. \end{aligned}\]
  • \(\widetilde g_j^{i,l,t}\) is agent \(i\)’s estimate of agent \(j\)’s physical goal, and \(s^{1:t-1}\) is the observed state history.

These updates allow behavior to be interpreted in terms of both physical and social objectives, rather than attributing every action to a physical destination alone.

3.2 Estimating social policies of other agents. Updated goal estimates are used to predict the other agent’s actions. Agent \(i\) estimates agent \(j\)’s policy using the lower-level Q-function:

\[\begin{aligned} &\widetilde\psi_j^{i,l-1} \left(s,a_J,\widetilde\chi_{jJ}^{i,l},\widetilde g_j^{i,l}\right)=\mathrm{Softmax}\!\left( Q_j^{l-1}\left(s,a_J,\widetilde\chi_{jJ}^{i,l},\widetilde g_j^{i,l}\right) \right). \end{aligned}\]

The softmax uses a temperature parameter \(\tau\) to control how strongly predicted actions favor higher values. Evaluating agent \(j\) at level \(l-1\) requires modeling agent \(i\) at level \(l-2\), continuing until a level 0 MDP is reached.

3.3 Recursive planning procedure. The nesting levels determine what the agent can reason about:

Reasoning level Model of the other agent Social reasoning enabled
Level 0 No nested social model; solve a regular MDP. Pursue a physical goal.
Level 1 Treat the other agent as a level 0 agent. Help or hinder the other agent’s physical goal.
Level 2 Treat the other agent as a level 1 agent. Account for the other agent’s social intentions, such as an attempt to help or hinder oneself.

At level 0, the agent solves a regular MDP. At higher levels, it updates the other agent’s goal estimates, recursively computes lower-level policies for candidate goals, and uses those estimates to calculate its own reward and action values. It then selects its own action by maximizing expected value over the other agent’s possible goals and actions. This process repeats at each time step as new behavior is observed.

Experiments

1. Setup The experiments use a virtual 2-agent grid world . There are six things in each scene: a red robot, a yellow robot, a red water bucket, a yellow water bucket, a tree, and a flower. A robot waters a plant by pushing a water bucket to it. The yellow robot pushes the yellow bucket twice as fast as the red bucket, and the red robot is the other way around. The physical goal is to water the plant by yourself, not just to have the plant watered.

2. Scenarios The paper tests 98 scenarios. They cover:

  • the same or different physical goals for the two robots,
  • hinder, help, or neutral social goals,
  • a physical/social scaling factor of \(-2, -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 1,\) or \(2\).

Negative values mean hindering and positive values mean helping. In class, the presenters explained a few of these values:

  • \(-2\): very unhelpful.
  • \(0\): the robot does not care about the other robot’s physical goal at all.
  • \(0.5\): it cares a little.
  • \(1\): it weighs the physical and the social goal about the same.
  • \(2\): very helpful.

Each scenario is run with level 1 and level 2 reasoning, mainly from the point of view of the yellow robot. At level 1, the yellow robot assumes the red robot has a physical goal, but does not know its social goal. At level 2, the yellow robot also tries to guess the red robot’s social goal.

3. Example In the example from the slides, the red robot has the flower as its physical goal and a social goal of 2. The yellow robot has the tree as its physical goal and a social goal of 0. With level 1 reasoning, the yellow robot is a bit confused about what the red robot is trying to do. With level 2 reasoning, the yellow robot infers that the red robot is trying to help. It meets the red robot partway, so it does not have to take as many steps, and it finishes faster.

In the motivation part, the presenters also showed a video where both robots want to water the tree and both want to hinder the other. When the yellow robot cannot model the red robot’s social goal, it gets very close to watering the tree with the red bucket. Then it sees the red robot pushing the yellow bucket, and it does not understand that the red robot is pushing away the bucket that is easier for it to push. It chases after the red robot, and the red robot comes back and waters the tree first. When the yellow robot can model the red robot’s social goal, it just pushes the red bucket right to the tree from the beginning.

4. Human evaluation Twelve human subjects watched the videos of all scenarios at both levels, \(98 \times 2 = 196\) videos. They rated what they saw as the robots’ physical and social goals. These ratings were compared with the estimates of the yellow robot in Social MDP, and with two baselines: inverse planning and a cue-based model. The cue-based model is basically a supervised learning approach. Because this is a virtual environment, the ground truth goals are also known.

5. Results

  • Social MDP matches humans well. Its correlation with the human ratings is high, while the two baselines do pretty poorly.
  • Looking at each time step, at the beginning nobody is really sure what is happening. As more steps are seen, the estimates lean toward one answer. In the example shown, the physical goal is probably the flower, and the social goal moves toward hindering the yellow robot.
  • For the social goal, the human scores and Social MDP are much closer to the ground truth than inverse planning and the cue-based model.
  • For the physical goal alone, the presenters noted that inverse planning seems to do better.

Conclusion

Overall findings

  • Social MDP does zero-shot social recognition and planning. In comparison, the cue-based model needs supervision.
  • It has a strong alignment with the human mental model, as shown by the human study.
  • As the instructor said at the start of the lecture, the idea of this paper is that a mathematical formulation lets social concepts like helping or hindering transfer to new situations, without relearning the underlying mechanism.

Limitations

  • The environment is a simple virtual environment and is fully observable. The paper does not use the partially observable version.
  • All goals are predefined, which is not what we would see in the real world, where people’s goals may change.
  • There is a limited number of agents and environment objects, so it is not as noisy as the real world.
  • At each step, the model has to enumerate all possible physical and social goals, recursively. The presenters pointed out that this becomes very complicated, and likely intractable, in a real-world scenario. Approximations would be needed, for example sampling possible goals or using a neural network.
  • It was not tested with humans.

Even with these limits, the presenters saw Social MDP as a good baseline. The next paper gets into studies with humans.

HABIT: Human-Aware Behavior and Interaction Training Dataset for Robot Manipulation

Motivation

Large demonstration datasets helped robot policies generalize across tasks, scenes, and embodiments. However, these datasets are usually collected in human-absent settings, with the robot acting alone. Robots will be deployed in shared spaces such as homes and factories, where they need to follow cues, anticipate human motion, and avoid collisions. Training examples that omit these interactions provide little direct supervision for such behavior.

A robot-only demonstration can show how to grasp a tool, but it cannot show the exchange with a person receiving it. Likewise, a robot-only workspace provides no example of pausing for a reaching hand. HABIT solves this issue by collecting manipulation demonstrations with a human present in the workspace.

Key ideas

HABIT introduces human presence as a new axis of data diversity. Every episode has a co-present human sharing the workspace. Tasks are organized into three roles: Collaborator, Coworker, and Supervisor. Directed subtask graphs keep demonstrations consistent, and the collection protocol elicits reactive interaction, yielding, tempo variation, and gesture grounding. The paper evaluates the resulting data by fine-tuning two existing VLA models and comparing them with models trained on matched Robot-only demonstrations where that baseline is applicable.

Background

Open X-Embodiment scales across robot platforms. DROID, BridgeData V2, and RH20T scale across scenes, tasks, and embodiments, while AgiBot World and RoboCOIN include bimanual, humanoid, and multi-platform data. Ego4D, Ego-Exo4D, and EgoVerse provide human egocentric video without paired robot actions. In class, a question about Ego4D clarified that it also has interaction splits. HABIT collects human-and-robot demonstrations with robot actions.

A vision-language-action model (VLA) takes camera images, language instructions, and robot state as input and outputs an action chunk. It usually includes a pretrained VLM backbone and an action head. The two examples are π₀.₅ and GR00T N1.6. π₀.₅ uses a PaliGemma backbone with a SigLIP image encoder. GR00T N1.6 uses an Eagle-Block2A-2B-v2 VLM backbone and a diffusion-transformer action head trained with flow matching.

HRI role taxonomies describe goal sharing, task sharing, and team hierarchy. HABIT adopts the Collaborator, Coworker, and Supervisor roles. In HARMONIC, the human teleoperates the robot as a tool for the assistive task. In LiHRA, the robot executes pre-scripted motions, and the data is used for safety-risk monitoring. HABIT records a robot perceiving and responding to an independent human with their own goals and actions.

Collaborator tasks involve a joint task with direct physical interaction, such as a handover. Coworker tasks involve largely independent activities in a shared workspace, such as working at the cashier and making coffee, while avoiding collisions. In Supervisor tasks, the human directs and the robot executes, for example by following a pointing gesture. There are 20 tasks per role, with one human and one robot per episode.

Task workflow

To keep demonstrations consistent across the roles, HABIT uses a task workflow. An instruction alone can be too ambiguous. For tasks such as ‘clean the shelf with a duster together,’ demonstrations can differ in how the subtasks are divided and ordered. The workflow is a directed graph whose nodes are human subtasks \(H_i\) or robot subtasks \(R_i\). Edges specify the order in which subtasks must happen. Both operators follow the plan during collection.

A single-agent edge connects two subtasks of the same agent, while a cross-agent edge connects a human subtask and a robot subtask. Collaborator and Supervisor workflows contain mostly cross-agent edges because robot steps depend on human steps. Coworker workflows contain mostly single-agent edges, with two independent subtask chains sharing the workspace.

Principles

There are two main principles of data collection. The first principle is reactive interaction. It uses a triggering cue. This is a visible human action that signals the start of the robot’s next subtask. Examples include pointing at a bin, setting down a coaster, or holding out a cup. Both operators know the workflow, so the robot operator could start reaching for the bin before the human points. The robot then moves without a visible trigger in the demonstration.

As a result, each operator acts only after observing the partner’s behavior, with no talking, countdowns, or other signals that the cameras do not record. Behavior cloning learns to predict an action from the camera view \(o_t\) and instruction \(\ell\); the operator’s memory is not part of that input.

The second principle is to elicit human-aware behaviors. For safety-first yielding, the robot operator decisively retracts the arms when the robot is about to contact the human or a human-held object. The demonstrations record yielding as the default response rather than finishing the original trajectory.

The human’s movement speed is varied across episodes to encourage the policy to match the partner’s tempo. For gesture grounding, the waiting time before the human points is sampled from predefined bins, such as 0, 1-5, 5-10, 10-20, and 20-30 seconds. This encourages the policy to wait for and read the gesture instead of acting from the language instruction alone.

For diversification, clothing colors are varied, object order is randomized, and operators with different body types are included across tasks. These changes are intended to reduce reliance on incidental features of the human.

Setup

Workspace setup

The authors used a a bimanual robot with two Franka Research 3 arms and Robotiq grippers teleoperated with Meta Quest 3 controllers (DROID-based). The front table was shared between humans and the robot, while the side table was only used by humans. Five synced RGB cameras (640×480 at 10 Hz) were used, in which two wrist (125° FoV) and one center (100°) on the robot side, while for the human side, one head-mounted and one exocentric cameras were used. The training process used only the 3 robot-side views; all 5 are released.

The following points show an overview of HABIT:

  • 10,563 episodes, 164 hours of bimanual manipulation;
  • 60 tasks, 20 per role. (Episodes: Collaborator 3,198; Coworker 3,969; Supervisor 3,396);
  • 308 unique human–robot pairs: 157 robot + 182 human subtasks (Both human and robot subtasks are annotated);
  • Avg. 3.67 robot and 4.30 human subtasks per episode;
  • Mean episode length 59.9 s.

Measuring success with a human present

Each robot subtask is scored on three binary criteria. The first metric measures whether the robot reaches the intended object state (manipulation score); the second metric measures whether states are reached in a correct order and synchronized timing, and whether it follows the cues (workflow compliance); the last metric measures whether the robot has contact with the human or human-held objects (human safety score). A trial $\tau$ succeeds if every robot subtask passes all three.

Experimental Setup

The goal of the experiment is to evaluate if the HABIT dataset improves task success rates and elicits human-aware behaviors (as compared to conventional data), so the authors tested two fine-tuned, open-source VLA models. They chose a “Robot-only” baseline for comparison: aka demos collected using the same task and environment as HABIT, minus the human operator. All models were tested on a subset of six tasks spanning 3 interaction roles: Collaborator, Coworker, and Supervisor.

Results

The authors derived the following interesting findings from the experiment results. First, training on HABIT improved task success rates over the robot-only baseline on every comparable task for both VLAs, which validates the effectiveness of their method. Among these, the most significant gains occurred in Coworker tasks, where (the authors claimed) models learned reactive yielding to resolve path conflicts in overlapping workspaces. Second, they revealed a pattern that HABIT allowed the models to successfully use the human’s pointing gesture as a co-located visual cue during complex, two-stage Supervisor tasks. For example, in the “food storage” task (requiring the human pointing gesture correlating to the robot choosing the correct container) models outperformed those trained on robot-only data. They also uncovered a reduction in pointing failures for HABIT.

Failure Analysis

Experiments identified that failure modes in shared environments extend beyond simple manipulation errors and are tied to the human’s role:

  • Precondition violations (box packaging)
  • Collisions in the shared workspace (donut serving)
  • Gesture-following failures (food storage) Accordingly, the authors found where HABIT makes improvement: training on HABIT substantially reduced these role-specific failures by teaching models to sync tasks with their human collaborators, yield to avoid collisions, and follow gestures.

Sample-Efficient Adaptation to New Tasks

In addition to the above experiments, the authors tested whether training on HABIT creates a strong prior for learning new human-robot interaction tasks, by fine-tuning the model on completely new tasks using limited demo budges (50, 100, and 200 episodes). The resutls show that mid-training on HABIT consistently achieved higher success rates with fewer demos than direct fine-tuning, and mid-training with 100 demos surpassed the performance of direct fine-tuning at the max 200-demo budget on both tasks (Shelf cleaning and waste sorting).

Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Robustness

The experiments also validate the robustness to OOD cases of training on HABIT. Specifically, “robust” here means deployed robots must be able to adapt to humans with different appearances from the original data collectors. Therefore, they assessed models against human distribution shifts, and found that core human-aware behaviors remained largely stable, while models’ ability to ground pointing gestures was more sensitive under OOD-human appearance.

Limitations

We summarized the following limitations of this study according to the presentation.

  • Environmental scope: All demos were recorded in a single environment.
  • The study does not discuss human operator diversity and its impact.
  • Workspace density: Interactions are limited to one human present.
  • Camera utilization: We cannot expect humans to walk around with head-mounted cameras constantly.
  • Evaluation reproducibility: For the experiments, it is difficult to exactly reproduce conditions of original experiment due to dynamics of real-world robot evaluation.

Discussion Questions:

  • Social MDPs use a linear weight X on the other agent’s reward (negative means hinder, positive means help). Do you think there are real social behaviors can’t be captured by a linear weighting?

    Linear weighting does not fully capture all of social behaviors. Dynamic linear weight may be a solution to improve robustness. Conditional and context-dependent social goal “Help unless it costs me more than X” , for example, can’t be represented with a fixed weight. But, altering the reward function could be a solution.

    We also discussed putting nonlinear operation in reward function may help. But it will result in the complexity of computing your reward function.

  • One way to build social robots is to put structure in explicitly (model-driven). Another is to learn behavior from large amounts of interaction data, as with learned policies trained on demonstrations (data-driven). Which approach is likely to generalize better to new people and situations?

    Model-driven approaches work well on specific situation but fail to generalize the variances of the same task. Combining method may create a possibility for better generalizations. Each generalizes along a different axis, and a hybrid approach is likely the best

  • HABIT’s data protocol treats acting before the human is ready as a failure (precondition violation), and operators are told to act only in reaction to their partner. However, some robot policies anticipate human actions and act early, thus reducing waiting time. What separates good anticipation from a violation? Does reactive-only data cap how fluent a robot can be?

    Good anticipation means preparing reversible actions while delaying irreversible ones until the human’s intent is clear. Reactive-only will encourage grounded behavior, but may limit fluency.

    Sometimes you may not wanna robot to anticipate. Because robots may fail to anticipate and infer human behavior. It is also very risky for robot to act before human since it does not act optimally most of the time.

  • Training a VLA on human-present demonstrations improves results but doesn’t solve collaboration. Collaborator tasks stay low and precondition violations persist. What is missing from today’s VLAs for working with people? Are VLAs the right architecture for collaborative tasks?

    VLAs provide a strong perception-to-action foundation, but often lack explicit representations of a human partner, task state, and temporal preconditions.
