entry.title: Preference, Influence
entry.content:
All authors are affiliated with the University of Virginia.

Introduction

This lecture report covers the Preference, Influence session in Learning for Interactive Robots (CS 6501, Fall 2026) at the University of Virginia.

Topic Overview: Learning human reward functions and preferences from pairwise comparisons, rankings, and active information gathering.

Incorporating Human Preference

Robots are often trained with data-driven methods that require large datasets. Instead, a robot can learn directly from human feedback (like how large language models are redined by prompting people which which response they prefer).

For robotics, such methods may include a human critic who compares a robot’s trajectories and a reward model learns from these comparisons. An RL algorithm then is able to train the robot’s policy based on predicted rewards from what is has learned.

This raises the following questions:

  • Alignment: Do we learn the correct preference? A reward function only sees certain features, so it can be difficult to capture everything a human may care about.
  • Sample efficiency: How much feedback is needed to learn preference? Every question interrupts the human, and humans may be inconsistent or dishonest in answering, so feedback needs to be used efficiently.

Robot Actions can Influence People

When robots and humans have to share the same space, the robot’s actions will influence what humans do:

  • Robot actions change the state: Humans have to adapt to what the robot is doing over repeated encounters.
  • Robot actions communicate intention: For example, an autonomous car may slow down to signal to a human driver to pass.

Overview of Papers

Both papers address one overall question: How can robots understand what humans want and what humans do?

What humans prefer: POLITE. Human preferences are usually written as hand-crafted reward functions. However, human preference is complex and these relationships cannot be represented in reward functions of this nature. Standard preference learning only says which trajectory is better, but not why. POLITE allows humans to highlight positive and negative segments within a trajectory to indicate preference and uses these as regularization terms during reward learning.

What humans intend to do: LILI. Most robot learning focuses only on single-agent tasks, but real robots work alongside other agents and people who adapt their behavior to the robot in question over repeated interactions. This paper investigates how a robot can infer another agent’s hidden strategy, and how to leverage this to influence other’s behavior. LILI uses an encoder-decoder to learn a latent representation of the other agent’s strategy, and then trains a strategy-conditioned RL policy that anticipated and influences other agents’ future behavior.

POLITE: Preferences Combined with Highlights in Reinforcement Learning

Simon Holk, Daniel Marta and Iolanda Leite

2024

Motivation

Research question: How can a robot learn a better reward function from human feedback when a preferred trajectory still contains behavior that the human dislikes?

Traditional RL depends on hand-crafted reward functions which struggle to capture complex human preferences, especially if there are several competing goals in one scenario. Preference-based RL allows for a human to compare two trajectories and says which one is preferred and why, which allows the robot to learn a reward function by balancing different goals involved in the environment and understanding the causal relation.

Example: A robot navigating a corridor has two goals. (1) it must reach the star target and (2) respect the people around it. Trajectory X reaches the star but cuts in-between the people. Trajectory Y avoids interrupting the people but misses the star. The human perfers X > Y, yet they do not prefer every part of X.

Problem with Prior Preference Learning. A preferred trajectory does not mean that all of its actions are preferred. Standard preference learning raises the reward of the whole preferred trajectory, so the undesired parts (like cutting in-between the people) are never punished. As a result, the learned reward function has flaws.

Intuition. Two kinds of human feedback can be collected:

  • The usual trajectory-level preference (X > Y)
  • Highlights that point out which parts of the trajectory were desirable and which were not.

Where both will be used to update the reward function.

Contribution

  • Proposed highlights, which can be positive or negative, that let humans mark desired and undesired sections within a trajectory to help agent learn causal relation.

  • Add highlights to preference learning as regularization terms on the reward model, which allows for finer-grained credit assignment.

  • Demonstrate better sample efficiency in simulated MuJoCo tasks and a better-shaped reward in a user study with real human feedback.

Related Works

Human-in-the-loop learning. Prior studies let humans give evaluative feedback as scalar signals , natural language corrections , or by segmenting a trajectory into desirable and undesirable parts . POLITE follows the same idea of allowing humans the chance to explain their choice, but builts it into preference learning so that the robot learns relevant information to avoid causal confusion with fewer queries.

Learning from preference: Preferenced-based RL learns rewards through active query selection , from scratch , bootstrapped with imitation learning , or from a pre-trained policy . In all of these prior studies, one label covers the entire segment. POLITE extends these works by adding highlights to show which parts of the segment are a part of the preferred label or not.

Methodology

Problem Formulation

Segments and Highlights. A segment $\sigma$ is a section of a trajectory. A highlight $h$ is a short windown inside a segment that ends at the selected state $j$:

\[h = \begin{cases} ((s_0,a_0),\ldots,(s_j,a_j)), & \text{if } j \le L \\ ((s_{j-L},a_{j-L}),\ldots,(s_j,a_j)), & \text{if } j > L \\ \varnothing, & \text{if no highlight} \end{cases}\]

where $L$ is the highlighted length, which is a hyperparameter. There are two kinds of highlights:

  • Positive highlight $h^+$: behavior that needs to be rewarded.
  • Negative highlight $h^-$: behavior that needs to be avoided.

Highlighting is also optional, so the human does not have to highlight any part of the segment in some cases.

Highlighted Query. Each request for human annotation is represented as a tuple:

\[hq = (\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \mu, h^+, h^-)\]

where \(\sigma_1, \sigma_2\) are the two segments being compared and \(\mu\) is the overall trajectory preference label (which segement is better than the other). The trajectory can have multiple segments, and segments can have multiple highlights. Each query contains at most one positive and one negative highlight per segment.

Goal. To learn a reward model \(\hat{r}_\psi(s,a)\) that agrees with the humans preferences for the trajectory and their highlights, and then train a policy on that reward function.

Framework

Preference Loss (same as prior work). The probability that the human prefers one trajectory over the other \(\sigma_1 \succ \sigma_2\) is the exponential sum of the rewards of the preferred trajectory over the total predicted rewards for both of the trajectories:

\[\hat{P}[\sigma_1 \succ \sigma_2] = \frac{\exp\left(\sum_{\sigma_1} \hat{r}_\psi(s,a)\right)} {\exp\left(\sum_{\sigma_1} \hat{r}_\psi(s,a)\right) + \exp\left(\sum_{\sigma_2} \hat{r}_\psi(s,a)\right)}\]

The reward model is also trained with cross-entropy against the human labels, for the error between the predicted and actual human judgment:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{pref}}(\hat{r}_\psi) = -\sum_{(\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\mu)\in\mathcal{D}_q} \mu(1)\log\hat{P}[\sigma_1 \succ \sigma_2] + \mu(2)\log\hat{P}[\sigma_2 \succ \sigma_1]\]

Positive Highlight Loss. The positive highlight loss raises the predicted reward of the highlighted actions:

\[\mathcal{L}_{+} = -\mathbb{E}_{h^+\sim\mathcal{D}_{hq}} \left[\sum_{l=0}^{L}\lambda^{l}\,\hat{r}_\psi(s_{j-l},a_{j-l})\right]\]

Negative Highlight Loss. The negative highlight loss lowers the predicted reward of the highlighted actions:

\[\mathcal{L}_{-} = \mathbb{E}_{h^-\sim\mathcal{D}_{hq}} \left[\sum_{l=0}^{L}\lambda^{l}\,\hat{r}_\psi(s_{j-l},a_{j-l})\right]\]

The two losses here only differ in sign. The discounted \(\lambda^l\) gives the most weight to the state at the highlighted moment \(j\). States that are further back in the window will count less, which emphasizes the actions close to the highlighted moment.

Total Loss. The highlight loss terms act as regularizers for standard preference learning:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{POLITE}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{pref}} + \alpha_{+}\mathcal{L}_{+} + \alpha_{-}\mathcal{L}_{-}\]

where \(\alpha_+\) and \(\alpha_-\) control how strongly each kind of highlight influences the reward.

Training Process. First, the policy is randomly initiallized and the initial reward model is trained. These steps are then repeated until convergence:

  • Step A: Use the current reward model to update the policy with PPO, and collect segments \(\sigma\).
  • Step B: Show pairs \((\sigma_1, \sigma_2)\) to the human, who will give their preference \(\mu\) and annotate highlights \(h^+\) and \(h^-\).
  • Step C: Add the queries to the highlighted query dataset \(\mathcal{D}{hq}\) and update the reward model with \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{POLITE}}\).

Experiments

Experiment 1: Simulation (Synthetic Feedback)

Hypotheses:

  • H1: POLITE is more sample efficient, so it needs fewer human queries than SOTA methods.
  • H2: POLITE converges faster than other methods.

Setting

Task: Walker2d and HalfCheetah, two standard MuJoCo environments in OpenAI Gym.

Feedback: A simulated human labels preferences with the true environment reward function (oracle). 10% of the labels are flipped to mimic a noisy human teacher. Highlights are generated by comparing to a threshold: segments with rewards above or below a set threshold are highlighted.

Methods: POLITE, PEBBLE , and a Preference Learning baseline (POLITE without highlights: \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{POLITE}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{pref}}\)).

The two MuJoCo environments, Walker2d (left) and HalfCheetah (right), used in the simulation experiments (source: Gymnasium documentation).

Main Results

  • Walker2d: POLITE with 200 queries beat the baseline with 800 queries and PEBBLE with 400 queries. With 400 queries, POLITE reaches nearly double the performance of the 800 query baseline.
  • HalfCheetah: With an equal number of queries, POLITE outperforms PEBBLE and the baseline.

Is this a fair comparison? Not really. A highlighted query carries more information than a plain preference, because it also includes which part of the trajectory was favored or not. Comparing methods by number of queries therefore really favors POLITE, as it is getting richer information that the other methods cannot receive without more queries.

Ablation Studies

Highlight vs. Preferences. The ablation study compares POLITE with highlights only and with preference only, each with 400 queries. Highlights only performs far worse than the preference only ablation, and combining both results in the best performance. The preference is the main learning signal, and highlights work as regularizers that refine these signals.

Experiment 2: Real Human Feedback

  • H3: POLITE learns a substantially different reward function and policy than baseline preference learning.

  • H4: POLITE is better at identifying and rewarding sparse goal states because highlights provide additional shaping to its reward function.

Setting

Social navigation. A simulated Pepper robot navigates through a corridor with three moving humans to reach a target. The study compares only POLITE and the baseline, using 400 preferences each. Both conditions start from the same pool or segments and preference pairs, generated by the same policy, but POLITE also collects highlights. 40 participants were included in this study for annotating; 20 for POLITE and 20 for the baseline.
entry.summary: Learning human preferences from highlights in reinforcement learning and intent from latent representations in multi-agent interactions.

entry.title: Intent/Trajectory Prediction
entry.content:
Introduction

Predicting human intent and future trajectories is an important problem in human-robot interaction. When robots work in environments with people, they need to consider not only their own actions but also how people around them may behave. For example, a delivery robot moving through a crowded area needs to predict pedestrian movements to avoid collisions and navigate safely. However, human behavior is difficult to predict because people can have different goals, interact with each other, and make decisions based on incomplete information.

This report discusses two papers that study human behavior prediction from different perspectives. The first paper, Social GAN: Socially Acceptable Trajectories with Generative Adversarial Networks, focuses on predicting multiple possible pedestrian trajectories by modeling social interactions. The second paper, Estimating Cognitive Biases with Attention-Aware Inverse Planning, considers how limited attention and cognitive biases affect human decisions. Instead of assuming that people always make optimal decisions based on complete information, this approach tries to infer what people may attend to or ignore from their observed behavior.

Although the two papers use different methods, both address important challenges in predicting human behavior. Social GAN focuses on generating diverse and socially acceptable future trajectories, while attention-aware inverse planning provides a way to explain behavior through underlying attentional biases. In this report, we review their main approaches, experimental results, and limitations, and discuss how these ideas may help robots interact more safely with humans.

Social GAN: Socially Acceptable Trajectories with Generative Adversarial Networks

Motivation and Problem

Predicting pedestrian movement in crowded environments is challenging because people do not move independently. Their future paths depend on both their previous movements and the behavior of others around them. For example, when two pedestrians approach each other, they may change direction, slow down, or choose different paths to avoid a collision. These different behaviors can all be reasonable, which means that predicting only one future trajectory may not be sufficient.

Previous methods have used hand-crafted features or recurrent neural networks to model pedestrian movements. However, many of these approaches mainly consider interactions within a local neighborhood. Another limitation is that minimizing the L2 prediction error may encourage the model to learn an average trajectory rather than multiple possible future paths.

To address these problems, Gupta et al. proposed Social GAN, which uses generative adversarial learning to predict diverse and socially acceptable pedestrian trajectories. The method also introduces a pooling mechanism to capture interactions between pedestrians and a variety loss to encourage different predictions for the same observed history .

Methodology

Social GAN aims to predict the future trajectories of all pedestrians in a scene based on their observed movements. For pedestrian $i$, the observed trajectory is represented as

\[X_i = \{(x_i^t, y_i^t)\}_{t=1}^{t_{\mathrm{obs}}}\]

where $(x_i^t,y_i^t)$ is the position at time $t$.

The Generator uses an LSTM-based encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder processes the observed positions of each pedestrian and produces hidden states representing their movement history. The Pooling Module then combines information from pedestrians in the scene to capture their interactions. The decoder uses the encoded history, pooled information, and a random noise vector to generate future positions. By sampling different noise vectors, the generator can produce different future trajectories for the same observed history.

The proposed pooling mechanism considers the relative positions and hidden states of all pedestrians instead of only using a fixed local neighborhood. These features are processed by a multilayer perceptron (MLP) and combined using max pooling. This produces a fixed-size representation that summarizes information from other pedestrians and helps the model learn social interactions.

The Discriminator is another LSTM-based network. It receives a complete trajectory consisting of the observed history and either the real future path or a generated prediction. It then classifies whether the trajectory is real or generated. Through adversarial training, the generator learns to produce trajectories that are more similar to observed pedestrian movements.

To improve prediction diversity, the authors introduce a variety loss. For each observed history, the generator produces $K$ possible future trajectories using different random noise samples. The loss is calculated using the generated trajectory closest to the ground truth:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{variety}}= \min_{k \in \{1, \ldots,K\}} \left\|Y_i-\hat{Y}_i^{(k)}\right\|_2.\]

Here, $Y_i$ is the ground-truth future trajectory, $\hat{Y}_i^{(k)}$ is the $k$-th generated trajectory, and $K$ is the number of sampled predictions. This loss encourages the model to generate different possible trajectories rather than making every prediction close to one average path. The variety loss is combined with adversarial training to improve both diversity and prediction accuracy.

Experiments and Results

The authors evaluated Social GAN using the ETH and UCY pedestrian trajectory datasets, including five subsets: ETH, HOTEL, UNIV, ZARA1, and ZARA2. These datasets contain real pedestrian movements in different environments. The model observes 8 time steps (3.2 seconds) and predicts the next 8 or 12 time steps (3.2 or 4.8 seconds). The experiments use a leave-one-out setting, where four subsets are used for training and the remaining subset is used for testing.

The prediction accuracy is evaluated using two metrics:

  • Average Displacement Error (ADE): The average Euclidean distance between predicted and ground-truth positions across all future time steps.
  • Final Displacement Error (FDE): The Euclidean distance between the predicted final position and the actual final position.

Lower ADE and FDE values indicate more accurate predictions.

The authors compared Social GAN with several baseline methods, including Linear prediction, LSTM, and Social LSTM. Table 1 presents the ADE and FDE results on the five pedestrian datasets.

The results show that SGAN-20V-20 achieves the lowest average ADE and FDE among the selected methods. The full model with pooling, SGAN-20VP-20, has slightly higher errors, but still performs better than the LSTM and Social LSTM baselines on average. The Social GAN results are based on selecting the best prediction from 20 generated samples during evaluation, while the baseline models produce a single prediction.

The authors also conducted ablation experiments to study the effects of variety loss and social pooling. The results show that variety loss improves prediction accuracy by encouraging the model to generate more diverse possible futures. Simply generating more samples from a model trained without variety loss does not provide the same improvement.

Although pooling does not produce the lowest displacement errors, it helps the model generate more socially acceptable trajectories. Figure 2 compares Social GAN with and without pooling in different pedestrian interaction scenarios.

The qualitative results show that the pooling-based model can better represent behaviors such as changing direction to avoid other pedestrians, moving around a group, and slowing down to let another person pass. The authors also report that the pooling-based model is approximately 16 times faster than Social LSTM in their benchmark, mainly because it avoids performing the same expensive pooling operations at every time step.

Limitations and Takeaways

Social GAN shows that pedestrian trajectory prediction can benefit from modeling both social interactions and multiple possible future movements. Its main contributions include the GAN-based prediction framework, the pooling mechanism for capturing interactions, and the variety loss for generating diverse trajectories.

However, the method mainly focuses on pedestrian movement and does not explicitly model environmental obstacles, scene semantics, or long-term human goals. Its prediction performance also depends on the observed trajectories of surrounding pedestrians, which may be incomplete or noisy in real-world applications.

Another limitation is the best-of-multiple-samples evaluation. Although generating several possible trajectories improves ADE and FDE, a robot cannot know in advance which prediction will match the actual future movement. Therefore, additional planning methods would be needed to use these predictions safely in real robot navigation.

Overall, Social GAN provides an approach for predicting multiple plausible pedestrian trajectories instead of relying on a single future path. It also shows why modeling social interactions is important for robots navigating in environments shared with humans.

Estimating Cognitive Biases with Attention-Aware Inverse Planning

Motivation and Problem

Understanding human behavior is important for robots and autonomous systems that interact with people. However, people do not always make optimal decisions, even when they know what they want to achieve. One reason is that human attention is limited. For example, a driver may focus on the car directly ahead but fail to notice an obstacle on the road. The resulting driving behavior may look irrational, even though the driver is still trying to reach the destination safely.

Traditional inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) tries to infer an agent’s reward function from observed behavior. However, these methods usually assume that agents make decisions using a complete representation of their environment. This assumption can be problematic when a person makes a mistake because they did not notice something, rather than because they preferred a risky action.

Banerjee et al. (2025) proposed Attention-Aware Inverse Planning (AAIP) to address this problem. Instead of explaining all behavior through reward preferences, the method models how people select information when making decisions. The main goal is to infer an agent’s hidden attentional biases from their observed actions .

Methodology

The method builds on Value-Guided Construal (VGC), a framework that describes how an agent forms a simplified representation of the environment when planning. Rather than considering every object, the agent selects a subset of objects that are important for making decisions. This subset is called a construal, represented by $C$.

For example, when driving on a road with several vehicles and obstacles, a driver may only pay attention to the vehicles that are directly relevant to the current task. This reduces the amount of information the driver needs to process, but it may also lead to unsafe decisions if an important object is ignored.

In VGC, the agent balances the usefulness of a simplified representation against the cost of considering more objects. This is described by the Value of Representation (VOR):

\[VOR(s,C) = V(s,\pi_C) + Cost(C)\]

Here, $s$ is the environment state, $\pi_C$ is the policy based on the selected construal, and $Cost(C)=-\lvert C \rvert$ is a negative complexity penalty for the number of represented objects, as defined in the paper. Thus, adding this term penalizes larger construals rather than rewarding cognitive effort. The agent prefers a construal that supports effective decisions without requiring too much attention.

The authors extend this framework by adding a parameterized heuristic bias function, $H_\lambda(s,C)$. These biases represent an agent’s tendency to attend to or ignore certain objects based on factors such as prior experience or visual salience. The probability of choosing a construal is modeled as

\[\pi_\lambda(C \mid s) \propto \exp\left(VOR(s,C)+H_\lambda(s,C)\right).\]

The parameter $\lambda$ controls the attentional biases. For example, a driver who is less likely to notice ice on the road may have a negative attention weight associated with ice patches.

Figure 3 illustrates how different attention biases can change an agent’s driving trajectories, even when the task and reward function remain the same.

The main task of AAIP is to infer the hidden bias parameters from observed behavior. Given a state-action trajectory $\zeta$, the method uses maximum-likelihood estimation to find the parameters that best explain the observed actions:

\[\lambda^*=\arg\max_\lambda P(\zeta \mid \lambda).\]

Because the agent’s construal is not directly observed, the likelihood is calculated by considering different possible construals:

\[P(\zeta \mid \lambda)=\sum_C P(\zeta \mid C)\pi_ \lambda(C \mid s_1).\]

Here, $P(\zeta \mid C)$ measures how well a particular construal explains the observed trajectory, while $\pi_ \lambda(C \mid s_1)$ represents the probability of selecting that construal at the beginning of the episode.

For more complex environments, calculating a separate optimal policy for every construal would be expensive. The authors therefore use a pre-trained Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) policy and mask the observations so that only selected objects are visible. This allows one policy network to approximate decisions under different construals and makes the approach more practical for driving simulations.

Experiments and Results

The authors evaluated AAIP in two environments: DrivingWorld and GPUDrive. Both experiments use simulated agents with known attentional biases, allowing the researchers to compare the estimated parameters with the true values.

The first experiment uses DrivingWorld, a simplified driving environment containing parked cars, ice patches, traffic cones, and a goal location. The agent must move toward the goal while avoiding obstacles. Three attentional bias parameters are considered, corresponding to ice, cones, and parked cars.

The authors generated behavioral data from 1,000 simulated agents with different bias weights. Each agent produced 125 trajectories across 25 scenarios. The model then estimated the three bias parameters from the observed trajectories.

Figure 4 compares the true bias weights with the estimated values.

The results show that AAIP can recover some attentional biases from behavior. The reported $R^2$ values are 0.77 for ice, 0.76 for cones, and 0.37 for parked cars. The lower result for parked cars suggests that some biases are more difficult to identify because avoiding parked cars is already strongly related to the task objective.

The authors also compare AAIP with traditional IRL. In an experiment with an agent biased to ignore ice, AAIP achieves a negative log-likelihood (NLL) of 265, while the tested IRL models achieve values between 513 and 537. Lower NLL indicates a better fit to the observed behavior. This comparison shows that changing reward parameters may not fully explain behavior caused by limited attention.

The second experiment uses GPUDrive, a driving simulator with scenarios selected from the Waymo Open Dataset. The experiments include situations such as lane changes, merging, and yielding to other vehicles. The authors use a pre-trained PPO policy to simulate driving behavior under different attentional representations.

In this environment, the authors generated data from 215 simulated agents, with 80 trajectories per agent across 10 driving scenarios. The attention model uses three heuristic features based on relative vehicle position, heading, and motion.

Figure 5 shows the results of estimating the attentional bias weights in GPUDrive.

The results show positive relationships between the true and estimated weights for all three heuristics, with $R^2$ values of 0.77, 0.76, and 0.83. These results suggest that AAIP can recover attentional bias parameters in more complex driving environments, not only simplified tabular tasks.

Limitations and Takeaways

AAIP provides a different way to understand human behavior by explicitly modeling limited attention. Unlike standard IRL, which mainly explains behavior through reward functions, AAIP considers what information an agent may have attended to when making decisions. This can help explain why a person sometimes behaves in a way that appears suboptimal.

However, the experiments are based on synthetic agents rather than actual human drivers. Although GPUDrive uses real-world driving scenarios, the behavior used for bias estimation is generated by simulated policies. Therefore, the results do not yet demonstrate that the method can accurately identify attentional biases in real human behavior.

The method also assumes known task rewards and predefined attention heuristics. In real environments, people may change their attention during an interaction, while the current model keeps the selected construal fixed throughout an episode. In addition, using a masked pre-trained PPO policy may not always produce optimal behavior under each simplified representation.

Overall, AAIP shows that understanding human behavior requires considering not only what people want to achieve, but also what information they use when making decisions. For human-robot interaction, this perspective may help autonomous systems better predict and respond to behaviors caused by limited attention.

Comparison and Discussion

Social GAN focuses on predicting where pedestrians may move by learning social interactions from trajectory data. In contrast, Attention-Aware Inverse Planning (AAIP) tries to explain why people behave in certain ways by modeling their limited attention. Social GAN can generate multiple possible future trajectories, while AAIP provides a more interpretable explanation of behavior through attentional biases.

During the class discussion, one question was how to combine individual pedestrian interactions with global crowd information. The class discussed using attention-based models, such as Transformers, to capture interactions across a scene. However, the professor pointed out that simply including more information may not be enough. Selecting relevant information is also important, especially when interaction data is limited. This also suggests a possible connection between the two papers, where attention modeling could help identify which surrounding agents are most relevant for trajectory prediction.

Another discussion focused on multimodal prediction and generalization. The professor mentioned that generating multiple trajectories does not guarantee that rare behaviors will be captured, since models still depend on the distribution of their training data. This helps explain why the variety loss in Social GAN is useful. The class also raised concerns about whether models trained on limited pedestrian datasets would generalize to different environments, crowded scenes, or people with different movement patterns.

For AAIP, the discussion focused on how attention may change over time and how inferred biases could improve safety. The current method assumes a fixed construal during an episode, but people may shift their attention as situations change. Examples discussed in class included driver warning systems and assistive robots that adapt to a person’s behavior. A related challenge is distinguishing between someone ignoring a hazard and knowingly accepting its risk.

Overall, the discussion highlighted that predicting common behaviors is not enough for safe human-robot interaction. Rare or unexpected behaviors may be especially important, even when they are not well represented in training data. Combining trajectory prediction with attention-aware modeling could be an interesting direction for future research.

entry.title: Human Models
entry.content:
Introduction

Topic Overview: Computational human models: Boltzmann rationality, bounded rationality, Theory of Mind, and belief modeling for human-robot interaction.

This lecture report covers the Human Models session in Learning for Interactive Robots (CS 6501, Fall 2026) at the University of Virginia. We explored how robots can understand, predict, and respond to human behavior when sharing an environment by reviewing two papers:

  • LESS is More: Rethinking Probabilistic Models of Human Behavior: Traditional Boltzmann models can assign excessive probability to groups containing many nearly identical trajectories. LESS corrects this by accounting for trajectory similarity, improving human behavior modeling and certain inference tasks.

  • Large Language Models as Zero-Shot Human Models for Human-Robot Interaction:Investigates whether pretrained LLMs can predict human judgments, trust, and social responses without task-specific training. Results show promising performance, but limitations remain in spatial and physical reasoning.

Why do we need human model?

Imagine a robot navigating a hallway with several people. The robot knows its destination and can detect obstacles, but it doesn’t necessarily know where people intend to go. The main challenge is that human behavior is uncertain. Humans can change direction, pursue different goals, and react to the robot itself. A human model helps a robot:

  • Infer intent: Understand what a person is trying to accomplish.
  • Predict behavior: Anticipate the person’s future actions.
  • Plan interactions: Choose safe and effective actions based on those predictions.

How do we infer decision-making and human behavior?

The lecture introduces:

  1. General Decision-Making Frameworks:
    • Markov Decision Process (MDP): Modeling sequential decision-making based on the current state, actions, transitions, and rewards.(agent always knows the exact, true state)
    • Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDP): Modeling decision-making under uncertainty by maintaining and updating a belief state from observations.(agent doesn’t know the current state)
  2. Human Behavior Modeling:
    • Boltzmann Rationality: Approximating human decision with a likelihood distribution
    • Bayesian Theory of Mind: Reasoning about beliefs of others with Bayesian updates

LESS is More: Rethinking Probabilistic Models of Human Behavior

Motivation

Human-robot collaboration requires a model of human behavior for both inference and prediction. For inference, the robot uses the model to recover human goals and preferences from observed behavior. For prediction, the robot uses the model to anticipate future human behavior and coordinate its own actions.

A standard choice is the Boltzmann noisily-rational decision model, which assigns higher likelihood to trajectories with higher reward. It was originally developed for decisions among discrete and distinct options. However, human trajectories lie in a continuous space with a continuum of alternatives that vary in their similarity to one another. Because the Boltzmann model does not explicitly account for these similarities, adding nearly identical, equally rewarding trajectories can increase their group’s total probability even though they represent essentially the same behavior. LESS (Limiting Errors due to Similar Selections) addresses this issue by accounting for both reward and similarity among available trajectories.

Background

Real-world trajectory spaces are full of near-duplicates. Consider two equally rewarding trajectories to a goal, one going left and one going right. Boltzmann assigns each probability \(1/2\). Adding two trajectories similar to the right-hand trajectory, with all four rewards equal, changes each probability to \(1/4\). The total probability of going right becomes \(3/4\), even though the added options largely repeat an existing route. However, the idealized LESS correction retains a probability of \(1/2\) on the left and reduces the probability of each similar right-hand trajectory to \(1/6\).

The choice rule comes from Luce’s choice axiom, which assigns each option a probability proportional to its desirability. For a finite option set \(O\), let \(v(o)>0\) denote the desirability of option \(o\in O\). The selection probability is

\[P(o)=\frac{v(o)}{\sum_{\bar o\in O}v(\bar o)}.\]

Letting \(v(o)=\exp(R(o))\), we obtain the Luce-Shepard choice rule. When the options are trajectories \(\xi\in\Xi\) (where \(\Xi\) is the feasible trajectory space), this becomes the Boltzmann model of noisily rational behavior. With feature vector \(\phi(\xi)\) and reward \(R(\phi(\xi))\), its continuous density is

\[p_{\mathrm B}(\xi) =\frac{\exp(R(\phi(\xi)))} {\int_{\Xi}\exp(R(\phi(\bar\xi)))\,d\bar\xi}.\]

For a finite choice set, the normalizing integral becomes a sum. Each alternative trajectory contributes separately according to its reward, so adding duplicates changes selection probabilities. Extensions of Luce’s model address this problem by grouping identical or similar options.

One such method is the Attribute Rule proposed by Gul et al. It treats options as bundles of attributes. Choice proceeds in two stages: first choose an attribute \(x\) using Luce’s rule, then choose an option \(o\) with that attribute, weighted by its intensity \(s(x,o)\).

LESS takes advantage of the Attribute Rule’s handling of duplicates while extending it to trajectories with continuous-valued features.

Less Model

LESS modifies the Attribute Rule by treating the feature vectors of trajectories as attributes. Trajectories with the same features are treated as a single option, and the group’s probability is distributed equally among them. If every trajectory has a unique feature vector, this exact-matching construction recovers the Boltzmann model.

However, real-world trajectories can be very similar without being exactly the same. Therefore, LESS introduces a nonnegative similarity function \(s(\phi(\xi),\bar\xi)\). This function is symmetric between trajectories and reaches its maximum when a trajectory is compared with itself. As a result, the model adjusts reward-based choice based on aggregate similarity:

\[\begin{aligned} D(\xi)&=\int_{\Xi}s(\phi(\xi),\bar\xi)\,d\bar\xi,\\ p_{\mathrm L}(\xi)&=\frac{1}{Z_{\mathrm L}} \frac{\exp(R(\phi(\xi)))}{D(\xi)}. \end{aligned}\]

In the equation, \(D(\xi)\) measures aggregate similarity to all available trajectories, and \(Z_{\mathrm L}\) normalizes the density. High reward still increases a trajectory’s weight, but similar alternatives reduce its individual weight. In the idealized left-right example, the right-hand trajectories share their group’s probability. For general trajectories, the adjustment depends on their feature similarities.

The paper uses Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) with a radial basis function (RBF) kernel to measure feature-space crowding:

\[s(x,\bar\xi) =\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\left(-\frac{\|x-\phi(\bar\xi)\|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), \qquad \sigma>0.\]

In this equation, \(x\) is a feature vector, and \(\sigma\) is the bandwidth, which controls how broadly similarity extends. Larger bandwidths make trajectories appear more similar. The paper fits the bandwidth through a KDE likelihood objective on sampled trajectories and approximates aggregate similarity by summing kernel values over a finite trajectory set.

Given a belief \(b(\theta)\) over the reward parameters \(\theta\in\Theta\), LESS predicts human trajectories by marginalizing over those parameters:

\[p_{\mathrm{pred}}(\xi) =\int_{\Theta}b(\theta)p_{\mathrm L}(\xi\mid\theta)\,d\theta.\]

After observing a human trajectory \(\xi\), Bayesian inference updates the belief over \(\theta\):

\[b'(\theta) =\frac{b(\theta)p_{\mathrm L}(\xi\mid\theta)} {\int_{\Theta}b(\bar\theta)p_{\mathrm L}(\xi\mid\bar\theta)\,d\bar\theta}.\]

For tractability, the paper uses a discretized set of reward parameters and finite trajectory samples.

Less as Human Decision Model

Before exploring whether LESS helps a robot, the authors explore whether LESS is a better description of how people actually make decisions than the Boltzmann model. They therefore designed and conducted the following experiments.

Design

It is difficult to test a decision model on real people, since the authors hardly derive one’s real reward function and hidden preferences. They avoid this problem with a browser-based gridworld study made of two trials, where participants make navigation choices on a grid world:

  • Control trial (a): one path is on the left, and one path is on the right, and both paths have equal length. Together with an attention test, this trial measures the baseline preference $\lambda$: the baseline choice ratio gives a relative preference between left and right without needing to know the exact reward formula.
  • Experimental trial (b): Two additional near-copies of the optimal right path are added to the same layout as (a). The right side now offers three nearly identical paths (labeled R1, R2, and R3).

It is the same duplicates problem from the Background section. Under Boltzmann, the near-copies inflate the denominator, while LESS treats the right cluster as roughly a single option. Therefore, Boltzmann predicts a sharp drop in the probability of choosing the left path, while LESS predicts minimal change.

Results

In the control trial, 47.5% of participants chose the left path. In the experimental trial, 41% chose the left path, while Boltzmann predicted 23% and LESS predicted 47.5%. The predictions are compared with the observed choices using a chi-square test:

Source P(left) in experimental trial Chi-square test against human choices
Observed 41% —
Boltzmann prediction 23% χ² = 6.27, p < 0.05 (significantly different)
LESS prediction 47.5% χ² = 0.72, p = 0.4 (no significant difference)

Boltzmann’s prediction is significantly different from the human choices, while LESS shows no significant difference from them.

Takeaway: LESS is a better fit for human decision-making, although neither model is a perfect predictor.

LESS for Inference

The user study shows that LESS is a better model for predicting human choices. The next question is whether a better behavior model also leads to better inference.

Inference with a Behavior Model

The robot keeps a belief $b(\theta)$ over the reward parameters $\theta \in \Theta$ and uses the behavior model $p(\xi \mid \theta)$ in two ways.

Prediction. Given the belief $b(\theta)$, marginalize over $\Theta$ to forecast human paths:

\[p(\xi) = \int_{\Theta} b(\theta)\, p(\xi \mid \theta)\, d\theta.\]

Bayesian inference. After observing a human path $\xi$, update the belief over $\theta$:

\[b'(\theta) = \frac{b(\theta)\, p(\xi \mid \theta)}{\int_{\Theta} b(\bar\theta)\, p(\xi \mid \bar\theta)\, d\bar\theta}.\]

The authors conducted two experiments:

Experiment Setting Manipulated factors Metric Main finding
Boltzmann & LESS comparison Simulated gridworld with two objects Sampling model × inference model; 8 rewards × 150 seeds TrueMatch, TruePosterior Inference is best when the inference model matches how the demonstrations were generated
7-DOF manipulator JACO arm, 12 users Inference model × sample set size (5 sizes, 10 sets each) KLAggregate LESS is more consistent for single demonstrations, while Boltzmann is more consistent for batch inference

Boltzmann & LESS Comparison

Setup. In a gridworld, a robot learns from human demonstrations about whether the human prefers to stay close to or far from two objects.

  • Sampling model: the simulated human demonstrations are generated by Boltzmann or LESS.
  • Inference model: the robot infers $\theta$ with either Boltzmann or LESS.

Each condition is tested across $8$ reward settings and $150$ random seeds. The following metrics are used.

  • TrueMatch: a binary metric that tests whether the robot’s most probable reward parameter exactly matches the true one.
  • TruePosterior: it tests the amount of belief the robot places on the correct answer.

The results show that inference performance is significantly higher when the inference model matches the sampling model. Additionally, Boltzmann is sensitive to feature density. (1) In high-density, the robot under-learns. (2) In sparse, the robot over-learns.

LESS weighs each trajectory by the inverse of its density, which prevents feature density from influencing inference strength. After LESS’s modification, the density is nearly flat, so it does not control how much the robot learns.

7-DOF Manipulator Demonstration

Real-world challenge. In a real-world environment, the denominator is intractable, so trajectory sample sets are required. Since Boltzmann is sensitive to feature space density, its inference results may vary hugely across different trajectory sample sets. This experiment therefore measures robustness across sample sets.

Settings. $12$ participants interact with a 7 degree of freedom (DOF) JACO arm on three household manipulation tasks.

Metric. KLAggregate is the metric used to measure robustness. Specifically, it measures inference consistency across different trajectory sample sets.

Results.

  • Single demonstration: LESS is more consistent. In the laptop task, the difference is significant for sample set sizes $S \leq 100$ and disappears for $S \geq 300$.
  • Batch inference: Boltzmann is more consistent when all $12$ demonstrations are leveraged to represent an “average” user.

Limitation

The presenter pointed out three limitations of LESS:

  • Similarity depends on pre-specified features. LESS measures similarity between the feature vectors of trajectories, and these features are pre-specified, so feature misspecification is a risk.
  • Batch inference is less robust. In the 7-DOF manipulator demonstration, LESS is less consistent than Boltzmann for batch inference. It is also unclear whether it is also less accurate.
  • Simplistic datasets of human choices; more realistic studies are complicated by the lack of access to ground truth.

Large Language Models as Zero-Shot Human Models for Human-Robot Interaction

Motivation and Overview

Human models enable robots to understand and reason about human behavior, allowing them to plan their actions while considering their potential impact on humans. However, existing methods face two main challenges:

  • Limited flexibility and scalability of handcrafted human models due to strong assumptions.
  • High demand for human interaction data in non-parametric models.

To address these challenges, this paper explores the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) to serve as zero-shot human models for Human-Robot Interaction (HRI). The authors demonstrate that LLMs, pretrained on vast amounts of human-generated text, can effectively model human latent states and behaviors. However, LLMs struggle with tasks requiring spatial and numerical reasoning. Additionally, their performance is sensitive to prompt phrasing and structure.

To further explore the ability of LLMs, they integrate LLM-based human models into robot planning and evaluate them in two HRI scenarios: a table-clearing task and a utensil-passing task. The results show that LLM-based planning can mitigate human overtrust and improve task performance. Nonetheless, LLMs may need to be combined with low-level models that capture geometric and physical information.

LLMs as zero-shot human models

Problem Definition

Let \(s_t\) denote the environment state at time \(t\), where the environment contains \(N\) agents (humans or robots), denoted as \(a^{(i)} \in \mathcal{A}, \quad i=1,\ldots,N\). The interaction history is defined as

\[h_t = \left\lbrace \left(s_k, \lbrace u_k^{(i)}\rbrace_i \right) \right\rbrace_{k=1}^{t-1} \in \mathcal{H}\]

where \(u_k^{(i)}\) represents the action of agent \(i\) at time \(k\).

The goal is to use LLMs to model a human agent’s action or mental state, represented by \(z_t^H\), such as trust in a robot or the decision to intervene. Specifically, the authors aim to approximate the conditional probability distribution:

\[p(z_t^H \mid s_t,h_t).\]

A textualization function \(f\) transforms the environment state, interaction history, and set of agents \(\mathcal{A}\) into a textual prompt:

\[x_t = f(s_t,h_t,\mathcal{A})\]

The LLM-based human model, denoted by \(p_l\), then predicts the distribution of the target human property \(z_t^H\) given the prompt \(x_t\). The objective is to evaluate whether this predicted distribution can accurately approximate the true conditional distribution of human behavior or mental states:

\[p_l(z_t^H\mid x_t)\approx p(z_t^H\mid s_t,h_t)\]

Experiment Setup

Models: The prediction experiments compare DAVINCI (text-davinci-003, 175B) and T5 (FLAN-T5-XXL, 11B). DAVINCI is accessed through an API, while T5 runs locally.

Datasets: This paper uses two HRI-related datasets and a human-human social interaction dataset. Each dataset has a different specialized baseline, trained or developed for that prediction problem. The details of these datasets are shown below:

Dataset Prediction task This dataset is for Baseline model
MANNERS-DB Social appropriateness of a robot action, rated from 1 to 5 Evaluating whether LLM-based human models can capture the effects of physical and spatial features in HRI BNN-16CL2
Trust-Transfer Trust after observing robot demonstrations, rated from 1 to 7 Evaluating whether LLMs can capture the effect of interaction history on a human’s mental state Gaussian Process and Neural Network (GPNN)
SocialIQA Social commonsense reasoning with three answer choices Evaluating LLM’s ability to reason about human social interactions Fine-tuned BERT-large

Prompts: Prompts include task instructions, relevant environment information, interaction history where applicable, and a question about the human response. The LLMs receive textual descriptions rather than directly inspecting the scene images used in MANNERS-DB annotation. Example prompts for each dataset are shown below.

Metrics: The paper evaluates three aspects of a human model: the error in its predictions, agreement with human labels, and how well its predicted uncertainty matches the variation in human responses. These aspects are complementary: a model can predict the majority answer correctly while assigning an unrealistic probability distribution to the other answers.

1. Error score. Let \(n\) be the number of evaluation instances, \(y_i\) the target numerical score for instance \(i\), and \(\hat y_i\) the model’s predicted score. The regression metrics are:

\[\begin{aligned} \mathrm{RMSE} &=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\hat y_i-y_i)^2},\\ \mathrm{MAE} &=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\hat y_i-y_i|. \end{aligned}\]

The paper uses RMSE for MANNERS-DB and MAE for Trust-Transfer. For SocialIQA, which has discrete answer choices, the error score is instead the fraction of incorrect predictions:

\[\mathrm{ErrorRate} =\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{1}[\hat c_i\neq c_i],\]

where \(\hat c_i\) is the predicted answer, \(c_i\) is the correct answer, and \(\mathbf{1}[\cdot]\) equals 1 when its condition holds and 0 otherwise. Lower is better for all three error metrics.

2. Consistency with Mode (CwM). This metric measures agreement with the majority human label. Writing \(c_i^{\mathrm{human}}\) for the human reference class and \(\hat c_i\) for the model’s corresponding class prediction gives:

\[\mathrm{CwM} =\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \mathbf{1}[\hat c_i=c_i^{\mathrm{human}}].\]

For MANNERS-DB, human ratings of 3 or above are treated as socially acceptable; the majority of these binarized ratings determines the reference class. Trust-Transfer uses an analogous threshold of 4 or above, with a single participant rating per instance. SocialIQA uses its provided answer label directly. Higher CwM is better, with 1 indicating agreement on every instance.

3. Distribution measures. For a given instance, let \(q(z)\) be the model’s probability of human response \(z\) and \(p(z)\) the empirical fraction of annotators giving that response. The paper evaluates these measures only on MANNERS-DB, which has 15 ratings per instance; the other two datasets provide only one label per instance.

Entropy relative similarity compares the uncertainty of the two distributions. The paper defines:

\[S(q,p) =\frac{\sum_z q(z)\log q(z)}{\sum_z p(z)\log p(z)}\]
  • \(S(q,p) = 1\) indicates same entropy.
  • \(S(q,p) < 1\) means the model has less uncertainty than the human response distribution
  • \(S(q,p) > 1\) means it has more uncertainty.

2-Wasserstein distance compares the distributions while accounting for distances between numerical rating values. For ratings \(z_j\) and \(z_k\), its standard discrete form is:

\[W_2(q,p) =\left[ \min_{\Gamma\in\Pi(q,p)} \sum_{j,k}\Gamma_{jk}(z_j-z_k)^2 \right]^{1/2}.\]

Here, \(\Gamma_{jk}\) is probability mass transported from rating \(z_j\) to rating \(z_k\). The set \(\Pi(q,p)\) contains nonnegative transport plans satisfying \(\sum_k\Gamma_{jk}=q(z_j)\) and \(\sum_j\Gamma_{jk}=p(z_k)\). Moving probability farther across the rating scale costs more. Lower is better, and a distance of 0 means the distributions match.

Experiment Result

The paper’s Table I below reports error scores, CwM, and distribution measures across the three datasets.

The result shows that pretrained LLMs can capture aspects of human judgment without task-specific fine-tuning. DAVINCI achieves aggregate prediction errors comparable to specialized baselines, and the CwM results indicate that LLM predictions can approach or exceed average human agreement with benchmark labels on MANNERS-DB and SocialIQA. However, T5’s weaker performance on Trust-Transfer under the original prompts shows that predictive effectiveness varies across models and tasks.

Agreement with human labels does not necessarily imply a faithful representation of human response variability. On MANNERS-DB, DAVINCI produces lower-entropy distributions than the human ratings, whereas T5 produces higher-entropy distributions. Although T5 is closer to the empirical distributions under the Wasserstein metric, the specialized Bayesian baseline provides the closest overall match.

LLMs on Tasks

From a Text Description to a Prediction

The previous section defines the input prompt as

\[x_t=f(s_t,h_t,\mathcal{A}),\]

where \(s_t\) is the current environment state, \(h_t\) is the interaction history, and \(\mathcal{A}\) is the set of agents. The LLM reads \(x_t\) and predicts a human action, judgment, or mental state \(z_t^H\).

For a task with a discrete set of possible answers \(\mathcal{Z}\), the predicted answer can be written as

\[\hat{z}_t^H=\arg\max_{z\in\mathcal{Z}} p_l(z\mid x_t).\]

The robot first turns the situation into text. The LLM then gives a prediction about the human. The prediction can later be used by a robot planner.

Three Prediction Tasks

The paper evaluates this idea on the three datasets listed in the Experiment Setup. The tasks are different, so they test different parts of human modeling: MANNERS-DB depends on physical and spatial context, Trust-Transfer depends on the interaction history, and SocialIQA depends on social commonsense.

MANNERS-DB: Social Appropriateness

In MANNERS-DB, the model receives a text description of a robot action in a social setting. It predicts whether people will find the action appropriate.

This task is difficult because the answer depends on details in the scene. The distance between the robot and a person, the direction of motion, and the position of objects can all change the judgment. These details are easier to see in an image or a physical scene than in a short text prompt.

Trust-Transfer: Change in Human Trust

The Trust-Transfer task asks whether a person’s trust changes after watching robot demonstrations. The input includes information about what the robot did before. The output is a trust rating.

This task is different from MANNERS-DB. Here, the main information is not only the current scene. The earlier interaction history also matters. A person may trust a robot more after several successful actions, or less after seeing a failure.

SocialIQA: Social Commonsense

SocialIQA contains short social situations with three possible answers. The model chooses the answer that best matches normal human behavior.

This task has less physical information than the first two tasks. It mainly tests whether the language model has learned common social knowledge from text.

Reading the Results

The results are given in Table I in the previous section. DAVINCI is close to specialized baselines on several tasks. T5 performs differently across the datasets.

The results also show that a correct final answer is not the whole story. A human model should also give a reasonable uncertainty distribution. On MANNERS-DB, the predicted distributions from the LLMs do not always match the spread of human ratings. This is why the paper reports both prediction error and distribution measures.

LLMs Sensitivity to Prompt Structure

What Is Inside a Prompt?

The LLM does not directly see the robot scene. It only receives a text prompt. A prompt may include the current state, previous actions, task instructions, and a question about the human response.

Prompt part Information it gives
Task instruction What the model needs to predict
Current state Who is present, what objects are present, and what is happening now
Interaction history What the robot and human did earlier
Question The action, judgment, or trust value to predict

Why Prompt Changes Matter

The paper changes the wording and structure of prompts and compares the resulting predictions. The answer can change when the order of information changes or when important context is removed.

For example, a prompt that only says “the robot moves an object” leaves out many useful details. It does not say where the object is, who is nearby, or what happened before. A longer prompt can include these details, but a longer prompt is not always better. The information still needs to be clear and relevant.

A Practical Limitation

This sensitivity creates a problem for real robot systems. The same physical event should not lead to very different predictions only because the text is written in a different way.

A practical system therefore needs a fixed prompt format. The format should state the task, the relevant objects, the robot action, the human action, and the needed history. It should also avoid adding unrelated details.

Case Studies: Planning

Using a Human Prediction in Planning

The LLM prediction is not the final robot action. It is one input to the planner. The planner uses the predicted human response when comparing possible robot actions.

For example, the robot may need to decide whether to continue, slow down, explain its action, or choose a different object. The better choice depends partly on what the human may do next.

Trust-Based Table Clearing

The first case study is a simulated table-clearing task. The robot needs to clear objects from a table while considering human trust. The paper replaces a custom human model from earlier work with an LLM-based human model.

The goal is not only to remove objects quickly. The robot also needs to avoid actions that may lead to an unsuitable level of trust. A person who trusts the robot too much may fail to intervene when intervention is needed. A person with very low trust may interrupt useful robot actions.

This case study shows that an LLM-based model can be connected to a planning system. It also shows that the model is used at a high level. It does not replace motion planning or physical control.

Utensil-Passing Experiment

The second case study is a robot utensil-passing task with human participants. The robot passes utensils to a person. The person can respond differently depending on the utensil and the robot action.

The planner uses the predicted human response to select an action sequence. The experiment includes 65 participants. The paper compares planning with the LLM-based human model against a basic myopic plan, which only considers the immediate task outcome.

The LLM-based planner can make better high-level choices in this task. However, the system still needs other components. The LLM does not provide object coordinates, collision-free trajectories, or a safety guarantee.

Conclusion

The paper starts by turning an interaction state and history into a text prompt. It then uses an LLM to predict a human judgment, action, or trust state.

The three dataset experiments test social appropriateness, trust, and social commonsense. These tests show that pretrained LLMs can make useful zero-shot predictions in some settings. At the same time, the prompt experiments show that the predictions are sensitive to how the situation is described.

The two planning case studies take one further step. They use the predicted human response when choosing robot actions. This is useful for high-level interaction planning.

The method still has clear limits. Language models are weak at some spatial, physical, and numerical details. A complete robot system therefore needs both an LLM-based human model and other models for perception, geometry, motion, and safety.

Discussion Questions

LESS is More: Rethinking Probabilistic Models of Human Behavior

  • The experiments show that LESS sometimes performs worse than Boltzmann. Then, does that indicate that we shouldn’t consider trajectory similarity when choosing an action? In the real world, when should we treat similar choices as distinct options?

The reason why we should consider trajectory similarity is that sometimes different but similar trajectories do not necessarily change the probability of selecting a fundamentally different choice. However, in the real world, this becomes complicated due to the interactions, influences, or states those trajectories will have. For example, a small trajectory difference is irrelevant during ordinary lane keeping but critical near a pedestrian or another vehicle.

  • The authors used predefined feature vectors for computing trajectory similarity. Does this limit the performance of LESS? If so, how can we learn those features or extract them automatically?

Yes, it can limit the performance of LESS because its ability to model human behavior depends on the definition. We can learn trajectory features using representation learning or human labeling. But this always comes with an additional cost.

LLMs as Zero-Shot Human Models for Human-Robot Interaction

  • Since LLMs are only used to predict human behavior, does it matter that these models perform poorly on spatial and numerical reasoning?

Yes, if models fail on spatial and numerical reasoning. It may fail to understand the physical environment and understand the behavior of the human. If the LLM incorrectly interprets these quantities, it may mistakenly predict human behavior.

  • The authors observed that LLM performance is sensitive to prompt design. Would this limitation make LLMs ineffective as human models?

In human-robot interaction, a human model helps a robot anticipate human behavior so it can choose appropriate actions. An inaccurate prompt design may impede the process of robot to predict human.

  • The authors used very simple tasks to test LLMs as human models. But, in the real world, would LLMs be sufficient to approximate humans?

The authors show a promising result of LLMs as human models on simple tasks. However, it still needs lots of effort for LLMs to be sufficient to approximate humans considering the complexity of the real world due to uncertainty, dynamic environments and so on…

  • When interacting with humans, some people will do the exact opposite of what’s expected, ex: intervene for a whisk but not a knife, seemingly just to be contrarian. How can an LLM or Robot account for this?

It is always tricky when some people will do things in a way that is unexpected or in an untraditional way. I believe this can be solved with further learning and fine-tuning. However, you can never wake someone who is pretending to be asleep.

Appendix

For the Motivation, Background, and Less Model sections in the LESS is More paper, I wrote a Word document version of the report based on the slides and the recording. I then used GPT-6.1 Sol to convert the Word document into a Markdown file.
